We demonstrate the full pipeline by deploying this policy on a real robot without any real-world fine-tuning. Using only onboard depth observations, our humanoid picks up, carries, and drops objects—including boxes, barrels, bins, and balls—across novel instances, sizes, and initial configurations.

84ea2xeP60.a: Mobile manipulators must adapt not only to objects, but also to the spatial context in which they appear: where to position the base, how to manipulate, and where to look while navigating surrounding scene geometry. To address this, we present COWBOY, a scalable sim-to-real framework for learning such contextual whole-body manipulation. On whole-body dexterous grasping, COWBOY transfers zero-shot to hundreds of objects and diverse in-the-wild scenes, spanning cluttered tabletops, shelves, drawers, and other unstructured settings. Rather than learning scene adaptation directly with RL in simulation, a vectorized environment-aware whole-body controller (WBC) handles reaching in thousands of scenes by coordinating base-arm motion, collision avoidance, and active vision. Then, local RL experts are trained in local scenes for object interaction and can be reused across thousands of full-scene layouts. We distill these composed WBC–RL teachers into a single vision policy that controls the mobile base, arm, dexterous hand, and actuated camera from point-cloud observations. The resulting policy exhibits contextual whole-body behavior, automatically adapting base placement, camera viewpoint, arm trajectory, and grasp strategy to observed scene and object geometry. Videos are available at cowboy-manip.com

JwpvRd730L.a: Quadruped robots are expected to operate reliably in dynamic and unstructured environments, where unexpected motor failures may occur and severely degrade locomotion performance. Traditional fault-tolerant control methods typically rely on explicit fault detection or handcrafted recovery strategies, which limit their responsiveness and generalization. In this work, we present a damage-aware adaptive control framework that enables quadruped robots to achieve zero-shot locomotion adaptation under sudden motor failures. At its core lies a pain-inspired reinforcement learning paradigm in which the reward explicitly constrains policy behavior, forcing the robot to exploit actuator-health cues from the ontologysense module, and thereby promoting safer, more protective responses to faults. To improve robustness, we design a failure-probability curriculum that gradually increases the chance of motor failures during training. Evaluations under weakened-motor and locked-joint faults show that the resulting policy achieves lower velocity-tracking errors than SOTA reference across all evaluated fault categories. Comprehensive experiments in both the high-fidelity Isaac Gym simulator and real quadruped hardware demonstrate that our framework achieves robust, damage-aware locomotion, marking a step toward resilient and deployable faulttolerant legged robots.
JwpvRd730L.k: Quadruped Locomotion, Motor Failure, Reinforcement Learning

eioQ9vJ6Oj.a: While recent advances in perceptive locomotion have enabled humanoid robots to traverse structured terrains, agile parkour in highly discontinuous environments remains an open challenge. In particular, crossing sparse footholds and narrow support regions requires precise foothold selection, effective use of visual observations, and consistent alternating foot placement during fast transitions. In this paper, we present a perceptive humanoid parkour framework that enables stable traversal across terrains with limited foothold availability using only onboard depth observations. The framework features a saliency-guided temporal perception module that combines a saliency prior with gated memory. It retains informative depth features across frames, enabling reliable foot placement from partial observations. By introducing an alternation loss, our symmetry regularization encourages alternating gait patterns and improves traversal robustness. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly improves success rate and foothold accuracy on challenging terrains in both simulation and the real world. Across five simulated terrain types, our method achieves an average success rate of 92.7% and a mean foothold accuracy of 83.6%, outperforming Hiking in the Wild by 16.7 and 7.8 percentage points, respectively, while real-world experiments further demonstrate robust sim-to-real transfer.

2Z8xQxrlsY.a: Scalable robot imitation learning relies on large-scale heterogeneous data from diverse robots or body-free data, making Cartesian end-effector actions a key interface for embodiment-agnostic policy learning. However, end-effectoronly abstraction leaves Cartesian policies unaware of the deployed robot body, making them brittle under robot-specific constraints such as whole-body collision avoidance. To overcome this limitation, we present E MBODI S TEER, a trainingfree framework that steers embodiment-agnostic visuomotor policies toward zeroshot, embodiment-aware deployment. E MBODI S TEER keeps policy learning in Cartesian space while efficiently lifting inference-time diffusion sampling into the target robot’s joint space via forward kinematics and Jacobian-based updates. With whole-body collision-aware guidance over joint trajectories after each denoising step, the arm can be steered away from collisions while preserving learned end-effector behavior. Across 9 simulated robots, E MBODI S TEER reduces collision rate by 46.1 percentage points and increases task success by 28.5 percentage points over Cartesian-only execution; on two physical robots in highly constrained scenarios, the respective improvements are 90.0 and 36.7 percentage points. Our project page is at https://frankwang67.github.io/EmbodiSteer-Page.

NZrwlgnR4X.a: Hierarchical control scales robot behavior by separating task-level planning from low-level control. In dynamic, high-dimensional tasks, however, a fixed planner-to-policy interface can fail when contacts, balance, or disturbances evolve faster than high-level policy updates. Execution therefore requires choosing not only which low-level policy to run, but also which policy-specific goal should be given to it. We formulate this problem as policy orchestration: runtime selection of a policy–goal pair that is likely to remain feasible while tracking the planner target. We develop EPO, an energy-based policy orchestrator for modular goal-conditioned policy families. For each policy, EPO learns a composite energy over low-level goals, where lower energy corresponds to higher feasibility and more accurate target realization. At runtime, EPO refines each policy’s goal and executes the lowest-energy policy–goal pair. Because energies are policy-specific, new policies can be incorporated by learning their own energy models, without retraining the existing policies or a centralized scheduler. In simulation, EPO improves the empirical precision–robustness trade-off by refining policy-specific goals before selectively switching among policies based on energy scores. We further demonstrate sim-to-real deployment of the same frozen policies and energy models on real humanoid loco-manipulation tasks. The project website is here.
NZrwlgnR4X.k: Humanoid Loco-Manipulation, Policy Orchestration, Energy Model

qF26obIUEX.a: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires long-horizon coordination between locomotion and object interaction, as well as robust adaptation to diverse objects and noisy real-world observations. Recent approaches have shown promis∗ Equal contribution. ing results by learning loco-manipulation policies from reference motions or taskspecific rewards, but they often struggle to generalize across objects. We propose E VOLVE, a framework for learning egocentric vision-based humanoid locomanipulation through simulation-based demonstration editing and hierarchical visuomotor policy training. Given a single successful demonstration, our method adapts it to diverse objects by applying structured transformations to robot keypoint trajectories. These edited trajectories are executed by a task-agnostic lowlevel whole-body controller that tracks future target poses of sparse body keypoints. We then train a high-level visuomotor policy from the successful edited rollouts to enable real-world deployment. In simulation, our method generalizes across substantial object variations in size, shape, pose, and initialization, outperforming representative reference-based and reference-free baselines. We further deploy the learned policy zero-shot on real-world tasks. These results suggest that combining demonstration editing with hierarchical visuomotor control is a scalable strategy for transferring humanoid loco-manipulation skills from a single demonstration to diverse real-world objects.

X4i3kSa2kd.a: Building a low-latency humanoid teleoperation system is essential for collecting diverse reactive and dynamic demonstrations. However, end-to-end latencies in existing approaches consistently hover around 200 ms, roughly equal to human reaction time, that severely limits responsiveness and prevents tasks requiring rapid feedback. We identify position-only PD control as the root cause of this latency floor and propose ExtremControl, a low-latency whole-body control framework that: (1) incorporates scaled velocity feedforward in low-level control, reducing tracking delay by approximately 70 ms with a provably optimal feedforward ratio; (2) operates directly on SE(3) poses of selected rigid links, primarily humanoid extremities, to avoid joint-space retargeting in the control loop. To minimize retargeting time, we derive a closed-form Cartesian-space mapping that uses a single anthropomorphic calibration step to translate human motion into humanoid link targets, accommodating operators with varying body proportions. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical framework for selecting control hyperparameters, and validate the effectiveness of velocity feedforward control in the reinforcement learning for locomotion setting through experiments in both simulation and the real world. Building on ExtremControl, we implement a teleoperation system supporting both optical motion capture and VR-based tracking, achieving end-to-end latency as low as 50 ms — well beneath the threshold at which system delay adds a full human reaction cycle to the control loop. This enables a qualitatively new class of reactive behaviors, including ping-pong ball balancing, juggling, and real-time return, that are beyond the capability of existing teleoperation systems. Project page: https://extremcontrol.github.io/.

mMRhLrwLFx.a: High-precision humanoid control is limited by target-domain dynamics mismatch, where the same control objective can induce different realized motions under changes in terrain, payload, or actuator response. Existing methods either pursue zero-shot transfer through domain randomization or in-context adaptation without target-domain specialization, or require heavy adaptation pipelines that leverage target-domain data, such as model calibration, residual learning, or policy retraining. In this paper, we present FADA (Few-Shot Domain Adaptation via Dynamics Alignment), a three-stage Planner–Inverse Dynamics Model (Planner– IDM) framework for few-shot adaptation in humanoid control. FADA ﬁrst trains an oracle policy with privileged information and then distills the oracle behavior into a deployable Planner–IDM student through DAgger. At deployment, FADA freezes the planner and ﬁnetunes only the IDM using approximately 2 minutes of target-domain rollouts with standard supervised learning. Rather than requiring optimal demonstrations or rewards, FADA uses the paired actions and observations that are observed during these rollouts as supervision, aligning the IDM’s action generation with target-domain dynamics. Experiments show that FADA outperforms both in-context and end-to-end adaptation baselines, improving task performance under dynamics shifts and enabling real humanoid robots to execute diverse high-precision whole-body tasks. Videos and code are available at https://lecar-lab.github.io/FADA-humanoid/.
mMRhLrwLFx.k: Few-Shot Domain Adaptation, Humanoid Control, Dynamics Alignment

mjvsJNQuFV.a: Legged manipulators combine the mobility of legged platforms with the manipulation capability of robotic arms. However, arm-induced Center-ofMass shifts and dynamic disturbances make the system more prone to instability under actuator failures, potentially leading to falls, task failures, or safety risks. Existing fault-tolerant control methods mainly focus on locomotion alone, leaving the coupled problem of whole-body stability and arm reachability in fault-tolerant loco-manipulation largely unaddressed. To bridge this gap, we propose FT-WBC, a fault-tolerant loco-manipulation framework for robust whole-body control of legged manipulators under actuator failures. FT-WBC adopts a decoupled upperand lower-body policy architecture and introduces two key modules: a Fault Estimator (FE) and a Posture Adaptation Module (PAM). The FE predicts faulty joints from lower-body proprioceptive histories, while the PAM uses this fault information to adapt the base posture plan generated by the arm policy, converting potentially unstable posture requests into safe and executable base posture commands. Through this fault-aware posture adaptation mechanism, FT-WBC synthesizes compensatory gaits under actuator failures and preserves as much arm workspace as possible while maintaining whole-body stability. Simulation and real-world experiments show that FT-WBC significantly improves survival rate and workspace under weakening or locked failures, and transfers zero-shot to a real legged manipulator in the real world.

HWaigsXLaH.a: Learning a general whole-body controller for humanoid robots remains challenging due to the diversity of motion distributions, the difficulty of fast adaptation, and the need for robust balance in highly dynamic scenarios. Existing approaches often require task-specific training or suffer from performance degradation when adapting to new motions. In this paper, we present FAST, a general humanoid whole-body control framework that enables Fast Adaptation and Stable Motion Tracking. FAST introduces Parseval-Guided Residual Policy Adaptation, which learns a lightweight delta action policy under orthogonality and KL constraints, enabling efficient adaptation to out-of-distribution motions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. To further improve physical robustness, we propose Center-of-Mass-Aware Control, which incorporates CoM-related observations and objectives to enhance balance when tracking challenging reference motions. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world deployment demonstrate that FAST consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in robustness, adaptation efficiency, and generalization.

JhdmNwpT4o.a: General motion tracking and teleoperation offer a promising path to scalable humanoid skill acquisition, yet most existing frameworks are validated on compact platforms or without real payload interaction, leaving full-size humanoids with real payloads largely unexplored. Scaling to full-size humanoids introduces two compounding challenges: their larger inertia and tighter balance margins make tracking highly sensitive to noise, drift, and retargeting errors from commodity VR trackers, while their payload potential remains largely underutilized. We present HEFT, a heavy-payload full-size humanoid teleoperation framework that addresses both challenges. HEFT learns from deployable noisy VR references with physically plausible reconstructed references through Privileged Motion Guidance (PMG), and uses a Windowed Payload Curriculum (WPC) with expert-guided payload caps to acquire robust heavy-payload tracking. We deploy HEFT on L7, a 175 cm, 65 kg humanoid. The robot tracks motions including turns, forward/backward locomotion, and squats under payloads up to 24 kg.

gbchkYm28k.a: Visual loco-manipulation of arbitrary in-the-wild objects requires accurate end-effector (EE) control and a generalizable understanding of the scene from visual inputs (e.g., RGB-D images). Existing imitation and sim2real methods jointly learn both these aspects via monolithic end-to-end learning and are thus hard to scale. In this work, we bring to bear the best tools for each of these problems – large vision models for generalizable scene understanding and simulated training for accurate EE control – leading to an overall modular loco-manipulation system that exhibits strong generalization. Our core technical innovation is HERO, an accurate residual-aware EE tracking policy made possible by combining classical robotics with machine learning. It uses a) inverse kinematics to convert residual end-effector targets into reference trajectories, b) a learned neural forward model for accurate forward kinematics, and c) goal adjustment and replanning. Together, these innovations reduce the end-effector tracking error to 2.44cm, outperforming the strongest prior method by 5.5×. Our overall system operates in diverse real† Equal contribution. world environments, from offices to coffee shops, where the robot reliably grasps various everyday objects (e.g., mugs, apples, toys) on surfaces ranging from 43cm to 92cm in height. Systematic modular and end-to-end tests demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed design. We believe our advances open up new ways of training humanoids to interact with daily objects.

O7LrmASsJS.a: Achieving robust humanoid locomotion in complex, unstructured environments requires transitioning from reactive proprioception to proactive perception. However, integrating exteroception remains a significant challenge: existing approaches often fail to achieve high-speed, stable locomotion across diverse, unstructured terrains. In this work, we present Hiking in the Wild, an extensible, end-to-end perceptive legged parkour framework designed for robust humanoid hiking. Our approach maps depth inputs and proprioception directly to joint actions, without relying on external localization and mapping. To ensure safety and training stability, we introduce two key mechanisms: a foothold safety mechanism combining extensible Terrain Edge Detection with Foot Volume Points to reduce catastrophic slippage on edges, and a Flat Patch Sampling strategy that mitigates reward hacking by generating feasible navigation targets. Extensive experiments on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot demon strate that our policy enables robust traversal of complex terrains at speeds up to 2.5 m/s. Code and video demonstrations are available on the project page: https://project-instinct.github.io/hiking-in-the-wild.
O7LrmASsJS.k: Humanoid Locomotion, Perceptive Legged Parkour, Reinforcement Learning

l8hOz8loVg.a: Hierarchical pipelines for humanoid loco-manipulation typically pair a task-agnostic whole-body controller (WBC) with a downstream task policy. Such WBCs are often trained through manual reward shaping, which yields visibly machine-like motions; more consequentially, they are trained without the manipulated object in the scene. Object dynamics are instead approximated through randomized end-effector force disturbances, a proxy that fails to reproduce the distributed multi-contact wrench a real payload applies across the arms and torso, with the gap becoming critical near the platform’s payload limit. In this work, we train the low-level (LL) controller itself as an object-aware motion prior: a single policy trained via motion imitation on retargeted motion-capture (MoCap) references that span the core motion primitives of the downstream task, with the manipulated object physically present in the scene. This single stage inherits natural human-like coordination from the references and absorbs the realistic contact wrench at its source, while exposing the same compact task-space command interface used by command-tracking WBCs. A reference-free high-level (HL) policy is then trained on top, with its action channel anchored to the empirical envelope of the low-level training data so that it generalizes the priors to a long-horizon multi-stage task while structurally preventing queries that would push the low level off-distribution. We instantiate the framework on a Unitree G1 for bimanual box pick-and-place: the same deployed policy generalizes across object masses and dimensions, initial and goal poses, and reactively recovers from intentional drops mid-carry. Video: https://youtu.be/viR_ULnRDQQ.
l8hOz8loVg.k: Humanoid Robots; Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation; Hierarchical RL

kpX1KOfNI5.a: Acquiring objects in human environments is hard for humanoids: targets are partially occluded under egocentric viewpoints, and reaching them demands coordinated whole-body motion that keeps the target visible and reachable while the base stays stable. We present a framework for whole-body affordanceaware grasping with active perception that couples perception and action through a Perceive–Align–Grasp pipeline: belief-driven active perception resolves occlusion by treating viewpoint as an explicit decision variable; a point-cloud– conditioned affordance policy proposes whole-body grasps; and an affordanceaware alignment stage repositions the body to the most executable configuration. A key insight is that, on a floating base, kinematic validity is not enough: we curate training data with controller-in-the-loop dynamics simulation, rejecting 73% of kinematically valid grasps that would destabilize the deployment controller, so ∗ Equal contribution. § Project lead. † Equal advising. the policy learns kinodynamically feasible affordances. Trained entirely in simulation with zero real demonstrations, our system attains 87.5% real-world success on a multi-level shelf task, generalizes to novel objects, and holds ≥73% at every tested height. Beyond generalizing within its training distribution, the policy extrapolates spatially: at scale in simulation it succeeds at table heights well below any seen during training, indicating that kinodynamically filtered synthetic data grounds affordances in object geometry and whole-body feasibility rather than in memorized configurations.
kpX1KOfNI5.k: Humanoid Manipulation, Whole-Body Grasping, Active Perception

hFLtQusqPy.a: High-speed racket sports provide a demanding testbed for humanoid robots, requiring time-critical decisions, precise striking, and dynamic wholebody coordination. In badminton, fast-changing shuttle trajectories require timely contact decisions, while successful returns demand precise racket pose and velocity within a brief contact window and across a broad three-dimensional striking workspace. Human motion data provide valuable priors for such athletic skills, but usable badminton references are limited and imperfect. Direct tracking provides insufficient executable variation for diverse shuttle conditions, while purely task-driven optimization may produce unnatural motion. We therefore present a three-stage hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for dynamic humanoid badminton. First, task-randomized motion augmentation expands sparse annotated hitting events into executable target-conditioned stroke variations, forming a continuous latent skill space. Second, a high-level planner outputs continuous latent skill codes to compose these skills online according to the observed shuttle state. Third, a context-conditioned adversarial regularizer encourages more natural planner-level skill usage while preserving return performance. In real-world deployment, our system sustains multi-skill rallies with human players, including forehand, backhand, and highly dynamic jump returns. This is the first real-world humanoid racket-sport system to demonstrate multi-skill human–robot rallies including highly dynamic jump returns.

3Ex2nEGqHP.a: We introduce Humanoid Hanoi, a challenge problem for long-horizon humanoid skill composition that requires a robot to repeatedly sequence pickup, locomotion, and placement skills to rearrange stacked boxes in simulation and on hardware. This symbolically simple task exposes a weakness in a common modular humanoid architecture, where reusable high-level skills are learned on top of a shared, task-agnostic whole-body controller (WBC). While such a WBC provides a unified low-level interface for skill composition, it may not be sufficiently hardened to execute the full collection of learned skills under domain randomization and long-horizon closed-loop execution. We compare strategies for addressing this issue, including skill-specific WBC fine-tuning, residual low-level adaptation, and task-driven data aggregation that expands the shared-WBC training distribution with closed-loop trajectories induced by learned skills while preserving its original tracking objective. In our evaluated system, the shared-WBC approach achieves the strongest long-horizon robustness. A direct transition-smoothing intervention further shows that low-level controller handoffs account for a substantial part of the composition loss observed with non-shared controllers.
3Ex2nEGqHP.k: Humanoid Learning, Hierarchical Control, Long-Horizon Challenge

2Z9666X2B7.a: We study the problem of navigating cluttered indoor environments with a humanoid robot. Unlike conventional methods that model navigation as a 2D path planning problem, humanoid traversal in cluttered environments requires continuous geometry-aware whole-body adaptation, including coordinated arm placement, torso adjustment, and gait modulation for collision-free movement through complex 3D spaces. We introduce TANGO, the first whole-body visionlanguage navigation framework for language-conditioned humanoid traversal in cluttered environments. Given a natural-language instruction and egocentric RGB observations, TANGO directly predicts 29-DoF joint-space actions for downstream whole-body control. We train TANGO entirely in simulation by synthesizing diverse collision-free traversal behaviors via global path planning, kinematic whole-body motion generation, obstacle-aware motion editing, and RL-based tracking. This pipeline provides dynamically feasible action supervision for learning languageconditioned whole-body policies. In extensive simulation experiments, TANGO demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in vision-language navigation, while outperforming strong modular baselines in navigating challenging scenes requiring obstacle negotiation. Lastly, we deploy TANGO zero-shot on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, and observe robust language-guided traversal in cluttered realworld scenes without training on any real-world navigation data.

9kXz22fI7a.a: Imitation learning is a promising approach for training humanoid robots to both walk and manipulate, but it requires a large number of demonstrations, which are time-intensive and difficult to collect via teleoperation. Existing data-generation algorithms can automatically synthesize demonstrations for manipulators, but they are ineffective on humanoids because their high-dimensional composite action spaces involve arms, legs, and torsos. We present HumanoidMimicGen, an algorithm for generating humanoid legged loco-manipulation data. Our algorithm adapts contact-rich whole-body skills from a handful of source demonstrations to new states, generalizing across changes in object pose. By interleaving these single- and dual-arm skills with whole-body locomotion and manipulation planning, the method generates stable, collision-free data across diverse scenes and layouts. To evaluate our approach, we introduce a new simulated loco-manipulation benchmark containing nine diverse tasks that test humanoid loco-manipulation capabilities. There, we demonstrate that HumanoidMimicGen automatically generates large datasets for imitation learning and enables a systematic study of how data generation and policy learning decisions impact model performance. We show that whole-body visuomotor policies co-trained with HumanoidMimicGen data outperforms those trained only on real-world data by 20%. Benchmark, code and datasets can be found at humanoidmimicgen.github.io.

USXQ0bDfAz.a: Enabling humanoid robots to perform agile and adaptive interactions has long been a core challenge in robotics. Current approaches are bottlenecked by either the scarcity of realistic interaction data or the need for meticulous, taskspecific reward engineering, which limits their scalability. To narrow this gap, we present HumanX, a unified framework that compiles human video into generalizable, real-world interaction skills for humanoids, without per-task design. HumanX integrates two co-designed components: XGen, an anchor-centric data generation pipeline that yields physically plausible robot interaction data from monocular video and augments it to create a diverse, scalable training dataset; and XMimic, an interaction-prioritized learning framework to achieve generalizable interaction skills from seconds of demonstration. Evaluated across five distinct domains—basketball, football, badminton, cargo pickup, and reactive fighting—HumanX successfully acquires 9 different skills and transfers them zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1 humanoid. The learned capabilities include complex maneuvers such as pump-fake turnaround fadeaway jumpshots without any external perception, as well as interactive tasks like sustained human-robot passing sequences over 10 consecutive cycles—learned from a single video demonstration. Our experiments show that HumanX achieves higher generalization success than prior methods, demonstrating a scalable pathway within a class of anchorable interactions for learning versatile, real-world robot interactive skills.
USXQ0bDfAz.k: Humanoids, Whole-Body Control, Learning from Human Video

aq2hmhW0kU.a: Current approaches for humanoid visuomotor whole-body manipulation, primarily relying on teleoperation or visual sim-to-real reinforcement learning, are hindered by hardware logistics and complex reward engineering. Consequently, demonstrated autonomous skills remain limited and are typically restricted to controlled environments. In this paper, we present the Humanoid Manipulation Interface (HuMI), a framework for learning whole-body manipulation tasks across various environments. HuMI enables humanoid-free data collection by capturing rich whole-body motion using portable hardware. This data drives a hierarchical learning pipeline that translates human motions into dexterous and feasible humanoid skills. Extensive experiments across five whole-body tasks, including kneeling, squatting, tossing, walking, and bimanual manipulation, demonstrate that HuMI achieves a 3× increase in data collection efficiency compared to teleoperation and attains a 70% success rate in unseen environments. Project website: https://humanoid-manipulation-interface.github.io/.
aq2hmhW0kU.k: humanoid whole-body manipulation, data acquisition, robot learning

93leGzRaPV.a: Responding to rhythm is a natural human behavior but a challenge of high-dynamic whole-body control for humanoid robots. Existing motion generation models produce expressive but physically invalid trajectories. As a result, even an expert-trained tracker accumulates a feasibility gap on long sequences of generated dance. In this work, we present InfiniDanceRobot, a latent-guided closed-loop system that streams music-conditioned dance directly to a physical humanoid robot. To provide continuous motion generation ability, we propose a planner building on diffusion forcing with a causal receding noise schedule and cross-modal alignment. Then the latent-guided closed-loop optimization framework is designed to correct next-token predictions from tracker feedback during both training and inference. Experiments show that InfiniDanceRobot can generate expert human dance for the robot, producing continuous, physically plausible, and high-dynamic motion across diverse music styles and dance genres. Project page: https://jinluzhang.site/proj/infinidancerobot.
93leGzRaPV.k: Humanoid Motion Control, Music-to-Dance, Motion Generation

mday00WZFr.a: In legged locomotion, divergent components of motion (DCMs) have emerged as characteristic states for balance control. They isolate the unstable mode of the dynamics but, in existing formulations, apply only to reduced models such as the linear inverted pendulum. In this study, we show how DCMs can be more generally formulated as Koopman eigenfunctions. Whereas Koopman analysis typically targets eigenvalues near zero, which capture conserved or slowly varying quantities, our investigation leads us to deliberately search for unstable eigenpairs with large eigenvalues. The resulting Koopman DCMs are data-driven observables trained using only real-robot data. On a real biped, DCMs learned from one hour of robot data improve tracking of reference walking patterns. We further show how learned DCMs provide state-based viability constraints when combined with model predictive control.
mday00WZFr.k: Koopman Operator, Legged Robots, Representation Learning

PLNJ3a6Yht.a: Humanoid robots hold great promise for operating in human-centered environments, yet ladder climbing remains one of the most challenging tasks due to sparse footholds and handholds, complex whole-body coordination, and sensitivity to perception and control errors. We present LadderMan, a unified system that enables humanoid robots to robustly climb diverse ladders and perform manipulation under such constrained conditions. Our climbing policy is built on a scalable two-stage learning pipeline, where we use hybrid motion tracking to learn multiple climbing experts from a single reference motion, and distill these experts into a unified depth-based visuomotor climbing policy via hybrid imitation and reinforcement learning. To enable real-world deployment, we leverage vision foundation models to bridge the sim-to-real gap in depth perception. Building on the learned climbing policy, we further train a separate manipulation policy using a dual-agent formulation, allowing stable on-ladder manipulation via teleoperation. Experiments demonstrate that LadderMan achieves robust ladder climbing across a wide range of geometries, successfully transfers to real-world hardware in a zero-shot manner, and supports various manipulation tasks under challenging ladder constraints. Video results are available on the project website.
PLNJ3a6Yht.k: Robot Ladder Climbing, Humanoid Perceptive Loco-Manipulation

4uXhlSOnz5.a: Leg odometry relies on the assumption that the velocity of a foot in stance is zero with respect to the world, which makes accurate contact detection a critical subproblem. Many approaches classify contact using ground reaction force (GRF) sensors at the foot tip, yet these sensors are not available on all legged robots and remain unresponsive to disturbances such as slippage while the foot is still in contact. Approaches without GRF sensing instead rely on heuristic pseudolabels, model-based foot-velocity assumptions, or supervised contact learning. In this study, we propose a self-supervised representation learning framework for contact detection that uses only standard proprioceptive sensing (joint encoders and IMU) and requires neither force sensors nor contact labels. A denoising autoencoder is trained on kinematic features, a two-component Gaussian Mixture Model is fitted in the learned latent space, and its posterior is used as a continuous stance belief that scales the zero-velocity measurement covariance of an error-state Kalman filter. Experiments in simulation and on real-world terrain show that our framework yields the lowest odometry error among supervised and probabilistic baselines, and that higher pseudo-label classification accuracy does not translate into better downstream odometry. Our code and dataset are publicly available.1
4uXhlSOnz5.k: Leg Odometry, Contact Detection, Representation Learning

wALhOwQWnx.a: Reliable manipulation requires humanoids to handle changing contact with objects whose geometry and physical properties are not fully known in advance, making accurate motion tracking alone insufﬁcient. We introduce a system that adapts a humanoid’s compliance to the task and the contact it encounters. A vision-language model (VLM) generates task-speciﬁc compliance proﬁles from task descriptions and supplied geometry, using a learned force estimate to vary stiffness during execution. The Whole-Body Compliant Control (WBC2 ) controller realizes these commands through coordinated whole-body motion. The controller learns from examples of compliant motion. Our ablations show that including force and balance estimators improves stiffness control and motion tracking. The controller achieves a 2.5× wider realized stiffness span than a calibrated compliant motion-tracking baseline while retaining competitive motion tracking. Its force-dependent proﬁles achieve higher observed scores on key insertion and book reorientation than constant-stiffness proﬁles, with no observed advantage on cabinet opening.
wALhOwQWnx.k: Variable Impedance Control, Functional Compliance, Whole-Body Control, Humanoids

5b4j0e21aJ.a: Integrating locomotion and manipulation is essential for robot autonomy, but scaling standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) to complex tasks is severely bottlenecked by the slow, manual process of dense reward shaping. To bypass this limitation, we leverage Sample-based Model Predictive Control (SMPC) entirely in simulation as an automated, rapidly tunable expert to generate massive offline datasets. Because this data solves the fundamental exploration problem, we can train an off-policy RL agent using purely sparse task rewards, drastically reducing the time required to learn new skills and eliminating the need for manual tuning. Integrating this high-level agent with a low-level dynamic stability controller yields more optimal behaviors that strictly align with true task objectives, ultimately allowing the learned policies to surpass the original optimal control teacher. We validate the robustness of this sim-to-real framework by successfully deploying complex loco-manipulation skills across different morphologies, including an arm-equipped Spot quadruped and a G1 humanoid.

QLhHHolka7.a: Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (CRL) has seen recent success in a wide variety of goal-conditioned robotics tasks by learning structured representations of the dynamics. However, despite its success in locomotion and similar domains, CRL often struggles in interaction-rich manipulation. We argue that a key source of this difficulty is object-centric interaction, such as contact or grasping, that induces distinct changes in the underlying dynamic modes. In this work, we prove that manipulation can only be approximated by piecewise affine transformation and interaction-induced mode changes create piecewise nonlinear reachability structures that are difficult for standard CRL energy functions to represent and plan over. Based on this analysis, we introduce Interaction-weighted Resampling (IWR). IWR performs interaction-aware resampling around phases before, during, and after interactions, encouraging the learned representations to better capture the dynamic complexity around interactions. Across interaction-centric environments, including 2D dynamic control, robotic manipulation, and robot air hockey, IWR improves both sample efficiency and overall performance over prior CRL methods, with around 19.8% average improvement in simulation. Finally, using a sim-to-real pipeline with policies trained by IWR, we demonstrate the first real-world goalconditioned robot air hockey agent capable of hitting goals, improving success rate from 25% to 60%. Project Page: iwr.github.io
QLhHHolka7.k: Object-Centric Manipulation, Contrastive RL, Unsupervised Learning

sS9FjkKKsm.a: Learning-based quadrupedal locomotion typically relies on complex reward formulations that entangle task specification, operational limits, gait preference, and terrain adaptation within a single optimization objective. We instead treat these functions through distinct mechanisms: rewards for task specification, constraints for operational limits, energy minimization for gait preference, and exteroceptive perception for adapting energy use to terrain difficulty. We show that these components jointly enable efficient, terrain-adaptive locomotion, and that removing each component exposes a distinct failure mode. Our formulation removes explicit gait priors (including air-time, contact-count, and foot-clearance targets) in favor of emergent behavior. Compared to a conventional complex-reward baseline, our formulation achieves comparable terrain traversal while reducing cost of transport by 56% and operational-limit violations by 96%. The resulting policies transfer zero-shot to a physical Unitree Go2 using LiDAR-based elevation mapping. Project website with videos: https://sites.google.com/view/locomposition.
sS9FjkKKsm.k: Quadrupedal locomotion, rough-terrain locomotion, reinforcement learning, constrained reinforcement learning, energy-efficient locomotion

Tk1gtgOESR.a: Universal humanoid motion tracking is essential for enabling humanoid robots to perform diverse tasks in human environments. To capture the wide diversity of human motions, mixture-of-experts (MoE) policies have been widely adopted, leveraging dynamic routing to enhance policy expressiveness. However, we identify that divergence between old and updated policies can be misestimated during policy-gradient updates of MoE policies, due to their dynamic routing. Because most policy-gradient algorithms regulate policy updates based on the divergence, this misestimation can lead to either overly conservative or excessively large updates, which can yield a suboptimal policy. In this paper, we propose Mixture of Experts with Alternating Policy Optimization (MAPO), which alternately optimizes the router and the experts to avoid the divergence misestimation. MAPO consistently tracks 182 motions that PPO with MoE fails to track, whereas PPO with MoE tracks only one motion that MAPO fails to track. MAPO also attains the highest tracking success rate among the compared methods and the lowest tracking error across most error metrics, demonstrating its superior performance. Videos can be found on the project website: https://mapo-corl2026.github.io/MAPO/
Tk1gtgOESR.k: Humanoid Control, Mixture of Experts, Policy Gradient

IY6ti85pg0.a: Perceptive bipedal locomotion over sparse terrain remains a difficult challenge: model-based methods are precise but brittle to uncertainty, while model-free methods are robust but struggle to discover the precise, constrained motions required for precise locomotion where small errors can cause catastrophic failures. We propose a model-assisted reinforcement learning (RL) framework that combines both perspectives in three steps: (1) generate a reference trajectory using simplified models; (2) train a privileged teacher policy with Lyapunovguided heuristic reward shaping around that reference; and (3) distill the teacher into a vision-based student policy. We show that this model-assistance procedure produces physically grounded locomotion, improving sample efficiency, reducing the need for a complex learning curriculum, and achieving smoother locomotion behavior alongside stepping stone performance comparable to a model-free baseline. We validate our approach in simulation and demonstrate a deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot navigating sparse footholds with lateral constraints.
IY6ti85pg0.k: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Model-based and model-free learning for robotic control, Bipedal locomotion

JbpsGhdjs9.a: Reinforcement learning has driven recent progress in humanoid motion control, yet existing pipelines depend on costly MoCap data that lacks the geometric context of the surrounding environment. This decoupling of motion and scene leads to physical inconsistencies—such as contact slippage and mesh penetration—on contact rich tasks. We present M ESH M IMIC, a framework that learns coupled motion–terrain interactions for humanoid robots directly from monocular video. Leveraging 3D vision models, we jointly reconstruct human trajectories and scene geometry, then introduce (i) a kinematic-consistency optimization that denoises motion from visual reconstructions, and (ii) a contact-invariant retargeting method that transfers human–environment interactions to the humanoid. Experiments show that M ESH M IMIC achieves robust, highly dynamic behaviors across diverse and challenging terrains, demonstrating that a consumer-grade monocular pipeline is sufficient to train complex physical interactions under realistic deployment conditions—offering a scalable path toward humanoid autonomy in unstructured environments. Please refer to our project page for more details.
JbpsGhdjs9.k: Motion Imitation, 3D Scene Reconstruction, Reinforcement Learning

FK33gnkKgF.a: Reinforcement learning has become the leading paradigm in legged locomotion, enabling complex behaviors from backflips to parkour via massively parallel simulation. Under PPO’s non-stationarity, shallow networks remain the de facto architecture, supported by carefully staged environments; nevertheless, the representations learned by these policies remain poorly understood, specifically the relation to motion produced on hardware. In this work, we empirically study locomotion policies through the effective rank of the network Jacobian and show that conditioning rank on gait phase exposes representation structures invisible from a global rank. In particular, we find that architectural choices, namely observation and layer normalization with residual connections, allocate more than one additional dimension of effective rank to swing-dominant states than to stancedominant states, which is mostly absent in vanilla MLPs. Building on this, we propose practical recommendations to convert these into diagnostics for healthier and smoother policies. In practice, this results in lower joint jitter, up to 2x, not only in simulation, but also on a physical Spot. More broadly, our findings show that how a policy distributes its capacity across the gait cycle is closely tied to its health and sim-to-real transfer.
FK33gnkKgF.k: Reinforcement Learning, Representation Learning, Legged Locomotion

X7QOq3QotA.a: Generalizing learned locomotion policies across quadrupedal robots with different morphologies remains a challenge. Policies trained on a single robot often fail when deployed on embodiments with different mass distributions, kinematics, joint limits, or actuation constraints, forcing per-robot retraining. Prior works have approached this primarily either by scaling via training across real or generated embodiments or using large architectures producing transferable policies which are both storage and compute heavy. We argue that both of these approaches circumvent a key failure mode in actor-critic learning: a shared value function tends to average incompatible value targets across embodiments, yielding miscalibrated advantages. Addressing this helps transfer and reduces compute cost. We present MorFiC, a reinforcement learning approach for zero-shot crossmorphology locomotion which fixes this issue using multiplicative critic conditioning on a morphology latent. Trained with a single source robot with morphology randomization in simulation, MorFiC achieves zero-shot transfer to a total of seven robots, reaching forward velocities competitive with or surpassing those of scaling-based and morphology-conditioned PPO baselines; for example, it reaches 1.98 m/s on AlienGo, whereas additive PPO baselines remain below 0.65 m/s. MorFiC achieves this using a single training robot and approximately 2–3 hours of training time compared to tens or hundreds of hours required for scaling baselines training on multiple embodiments. We diagnose critic calibration via three metrics: explained variance, advantage sign-flip rate, and policy gradient cosine, confirming critic conditioning as a determinant of policy update direction. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot deployment on Unitree Go1 and Go2 robots without fine-tuning. Project page: https://prakharmishra27.github.io/MorFiC/

XJgz1iK29G.a: We present MotionDisco, a framework that discovers contact-rich, long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation motions from scratch, without relying on teleoperation or motion retargeting from human demonstrations. This is challenging because the space of possible contact interactions grows combinatorially with the task horizon and the number of objects in the scene. MotionDisco enables rapid discovery of novel motions by coupling a large language model (LLM) guided evolutionary search over sequences of interactions with an efficient sequential kinodynamic trajectory optimizer and pruning strategy, enabling the rapid discovery of novel skills. Through extensive ablation studies, we show that our LLM-guided search discovers successful whole-body trajectories across several challenging long-horizon tasks. Finally, by training reinforcement learning tracking policies on the discovered trajectories, we transfer the motions to a real humanoid robot. This is the first work to discover and deploy long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation skills entirely through automated evolutionary search. Supplementary videos of the experiments are available at: https://youtu.be/DHiVz34QYlw.
XJgz1iK29G.k: Motion Discovery, Humanoid Loco-Manipulation, Program Search

0HS0to0eVo.a: Reinforcement learning (RL) for locomotion frequently converges to locally optimal but undeployable behaviors, such as vibrating limbs or scooting on the torso, that maximize return without producing a usable gait. We present MPC-Injection, a low-overhead method that steers RL toward a designer-preferred behavior by inserting transitions generated in the same environment by a model predictive controller (MPC). Unlike reward shaping, MPC-Injection does not require redesigning the task reward, and unlike adversarial imitation learning, it adds no discriminator, no kinematic retargeting, and no auxiliary objective. We analyze how the injected transitions bias the learning, allowing the policy to converge to behaviors that pure RL may fail to reach under simple reward functions. On a 2D walker in simulation and with sim-to-real evaluation on a Go2 quadruped, we show that MPC-Injection produces gaits qualitatively comparable to those of reward shaping and adversarial motion priors. We also show that MPC-Injection can complete a barrel roll that pure RL fails to achieve under the same simple reward and can select between trotting and bounding gaits only through changing the injected MPC data.
0HS0to0eVo.k: reinforcement learning, model predictive control, legged locomotion

r27erS063s.a: Learning long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation poses a dual challenge: it requires not only the robust execution of meta-skills but also their seamless, closed-loop chaining equipped with autonomous recovery. Existing approaches remain limited: explicit humanoid-object interaction representations offer precision but are notoriously difficult for high-level planning, whereas implicit skill embeddings are compact but lack the interpretability required for reliable composition. We propose OmniContact, a hierarchical framework centered on contact flow (CF), a compact representation consisting of key body trajectories and time-series binary contact signals. Leveraging this shared interface, our lowlevel policy CF-Track learns a unified library of loco-manipulation skills, while our high-level module CF-Gen heuristically synthesizes future contact-flow sequences. To support this setting, we additionally collect the OmniContact dataset, a MoCap-based HOI corpus for humanoid loco-manipulation (Appendix A). Together, they enable robust execution, autonomous failure recovery, and flexible composition of meta-skills for long-horizon tasks. Experiments show that OmniContact achieves 92.7% success on Carry Box and 76.5% on Push-Stack Boxes, outperforming prior baselines by average margins of 42.9% in meta-skill and 66.5% in skill chaining. Besides, our framework naturally integrates with VLMs for semantic task decomposition, enabling complex, semantically grounded locomanipulation behaviors, such as arranging scattered boxes into a heart shape.

TTFZrb0Hw3.a: Whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating the robot’s entire kinematic chain. However, most existing systems typically decouple the upper and lower bodies into separate controllers, limiting such coordination and yielding behaviors similar to those of a wheeled dual-arm platform. In this paper, we ask what it takes to build a whole-body native vision-languageaction (VLA) model that maps language and pixels directly to all of the humanoid’s degrees of freedom. We conduct a systematic empirical study organized as a roadmap of one-variable-at-a-time experiments across three phases: wholebody teleoperation, VLA model design, and heterogeneous co-training. Our study yields several intriguing findings: a joint-based whole-body teleoperation interface outperforms alternatives that only partially expose the humanoid’s degrees of freedom; a VLA pretrained on static and wheeled dual-arm platforms transfers surprisingly well to a humanoid’s full action space; and co-training with HuMI, the humanoid analog of UMI, extends the policy to new objects and instructions without additional whole-body teleoperation on those targets. Following this roadmap yields OpenHLM, an open-source recipe for whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation. In a challenging long-horizon task that spans a wide vertical range of the humanoid, OpenHLM outperforms two state-of-the-art humanoid VLA baselines (GR00T N1.6 and Ψ0 ) using less than half the total demonstration time. Our code, training data, and model checkpoints are available at https://openhlmproject.github.io/.
TTFZrb0Hw3.k: Humanoid Loco-Manipulation, Whole-Body Control, VLA VR Control Signals

XA0dFQQlqP.a: Vine robots, a class of soft, growing robots, are suitable for navigating complex and confined environments due to their compliant bodies and selfsupporting growth mechanism. However, hysteresis, tether interactions, and deformations make them difficult to predict and model, which in turn limits the effectiveness of conventional planning and control approaches. In this work, we present a data-driven, vision-based control framework for the first autonomous vine robot system. Our system integrates 19 cameras distributed along the robot’s body to provide comprehensive feedback of both the robot state and the surrounding environment. Using this rich whole-body vision feedback, we train an end-toend visuomotor policy from demonstrations for closed-loop autonomous control in complex environments. The policy efficiently aggregates information from distributed sensing while maintaining robustness to inaccurate robot states and actuation. Experimental results demonstrate that the learned policy enables robust navigation and manipulation in challenging scenarios, including steering through branched structures, climbing up slopes, traversing unsupported terrain, reaching objects precisely, and maneuvering through confined spaces and obstacles. Project website https://panovine-bot.github.io.
XA0dFQQlqP.k: Vine robot, soft robot, whole-body sensing, imitation learning

lY47GBfn32.a: Motion imitation is a promising approach for humanoid locomotion, enabling agents to acquire humanlike behaviors. Existing methods typically rely on high-quality motion capture datasets such as AMASS, but these are scarce and expensive, limiting scalability and diversity. Recent studies attempt to scale data collection by converting large-scale internet videos, exemplified by Humanoid-X. However, they often suffer from physical artifacts such as floating, penetration, and foot skating, which hinder stable imitation. To address this, we introduce PHUMA, a Physically Reliable HUMAnoid locomotion dataset produced by a two-stage pipeline combining physics-aware curation and retargeting, aggregating both motion capture and internet video into a physically reliable, 73-hour corpus. On motion tracking benchmarks, PHUMA-trained policies achieve higher success rates than those trained on AMASS and Humanoid-X, and successfully transfer zero-shot to a real Unitree G1.

VKVM1q9FbN.a: Model-free reinforcement learning has enabled impressive humanoid locomotion; however, control on steep slopes remains largely unexplored. Unlike flat or discrete terrains, sloped terrains impose a persistent gravitational bias that demands simultaneous stability and posture control. Consequently, under generic reward formulations, policies can converge to slow, conservative lowcenter-of-mass (CoM) crouched gaits. In this work, we propose a novel twostage physics-guided framework, dubbed HumoSlope, dedicated to robust humanoid locomotion on diverse sloped terrains. Specifically, Stage I establishes a terrain-consistent balance prior by introducing a slope-adaptive Zero Moment Point (ZMP) regularizer evaluated directly on the local inclined support plane rather than a world-horizontal reference. To prevent the resulting policy from defaulting to a crouched posture, Stage II introduces the Biomechanical Slope Gait Adapter (BSGA). Utilizing extracted macroscopic terrain descriptors as priv ileged, training-only signals, BSGA dynamically gates soft reward priors to modulate CoM height and lower-limb coordination based on the estimated slope geometry—encouraging hip-dominant uphill propulsion and knee-oriented downhill braking. Crucially, the deployed actor remains entirely proprioceptive, requiring no online exteroceptive sensing. Extensive Sim-to-Real experiments demonstrate that our framework effectively mitigates posture degeneration and enables blind, continuous traversal of outdoor grass slopes up to 62.7% (32.1◦ ), validating a physics-guided approach to challenging slope terrain adaptation. Project website: https://xychen-hust.github.io/HumoSlope-CoRL2026/.
VKVM1q9FbN.k: Humanoid Locomotion, Sloped Terrains, Reinforcement Learning

XnyoJXimAK.a: Humanoid soccer requires a robot to seamlessly combine agile locomotion, ball manipulation, and impact-rich contact dynamics across a continuous, dynamic behavioral spectrum. Yet existing approaches either cover only a limited set of skills, or forego motion priors entirely and produce unnatural behaviors, leaving the combination of a unified skill set and human-like motion quality unaddressed. We present S OCCER B OT, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that resolves both limitations through a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. By constraining policy learning within this dynamically plausible motion manifold, a single skill-conditioned policy naturally learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking in a unified formulation, while inherently producing human-like motion and fluid transitions during commanded skill switching. Augmented by robustness-oriented simulation design, S OCCER B OT transfers zero-shot to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating agile, natural, and robust execution of the full soccer skill repertoire under real-world conditions.

rTX0zr5FjT.a: Robotic imitation learning requires policies that capture multimodal action distributions, run at real-time control rates, and exploit available sensors. Existing generative approaches, including diffusion, flow matching, and IMLE, satisfy these requirements only partially. We present PRISM, a single-pass multisensory policy built on a calibrated batch-global RS–IMLE objective. We show that the RS–IMLE rejection mechanism, originally designed for few-shot image synthesis, degenerates at policy-scale batch sizes, and introduce the calibration needed to restore effective rejection. PRISM couples a temporal multisensory encoder (RGB, depth, tactile, audio, proprioception) with a linear-attention Performer generator trained under this objective. On real-world loco-manipulation (Unitree Go2 + 7-DoF arm) and tabletop manipulation (UR5), PRISM improves success over diffusion, flow, and IMLE baselines by 10–25 pp while sustaining 30– 50 Hz closed-loop control. On language-conditioned CALVIN ABCD, it improves success by ∼31 percentage points over diffusion and ∼24 pp over flow matching, while reducing trajectory jerk by 20×–70×.1

rQZHMVTYYy.a: Robot policies map observations to actions, typically using multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). Yet robot dynamics and control objectives involve multiplicative interactions among observable physical variables. MLPs can approximate these interactions but must learn them implicitly, at a representational cost. We introduce PRISM (Polynomial Representations for Interaction-Structured Motor Control), a physics-motivated yet data-driven representation that learns multiplicative interactions by recursively adding scaled bilinear features, without enumerating all polynomial terms. Replacing only the MLP’s first affine layer, PRISM is plug-and-play for reinforcement and imitation learning, requiring no changes to training objectives, sensing, or controllers. Across humanoid locomotion and contact-rich manipulation, PRISM improves survival from 51.0% to 92.5%, outperforming even larger MLPs. More strikingly, its performance advantage persists under out-of-distribution changes in friction, robot mass, and payload, without retraining. PRISM also exhibits sensorless compliance-like behavior, increases failure-recovery success from 40.9% to 52.3% without explicit admittance control, improves real-robot manipulation, and learns features that better predict physical quantities. These results make PRISM a compelling alternative to standard MLPs for robot policy learning. The project page is available at https://lsh3163.github.io/prism/.
rQZHMVTYYy.k: Polynomial interaction, Motor control, Sensorless compliance

rK0JCfddwK.a: Reliable humanoid–object interaction (HOI) tasks are hindered by a lack of generalizable control interfaces and robust closed-loop perception. We introduce Perceptive Root-guided Humanoid-Object Interaction (Pro-HOI), a framework for robust humanoid loco-manipulation with spatial generalization capabilities. We design a policy conditioned on root trajectories and contact commands, using only a few box-carrying reference motions for tracking rewards. This design provides a controllable interface to generalizable interactions, which can also transfer to various other types of interactions. Finally, an objectestimation module fuses real-time detection with a MuJoCo Digital Twin to detect when an object falls and trigger re-grasping. Experiments on a Unitree G1 demonstrate improved spatial generalization and reliable long-horizon execution in real-world box-carrying scenarios. Video results are available on our webpage. ∗ Corresponding authors.

317SZV2vuS.a: Vision-based perceptive locomotion has enabled legged robots to achieve agile and terrain-aware locomotion across complex environments. However, the reliability of such systems heavily depends on visual observations, which are inherently susceptible to occlusion, reflective surfaces, and illumination variations, often resulting in catastrophic locomotion failures under degraded perception conditions. In this paper, we present PROOF (Perceptive Robustness via Out-of-Distribution Fallback for Legged Locomotion), a perceptive locomotion framework that enables robust locomotion under severe visual disturbances. Our method adopts a two-stage teacher–student learning paradigm that explicitly models perception reliability: the teacher learns both perception-driven and proprioceptive fallback behaviors, while the student predicts exteroceptive features with uncertainty and suppresses them under out-of-distribution inputs. We evaluate our method on a Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a RealSense D435 depth camera in real-world settings. Under normal visual conditions, our method enables the robot to successfully perform high-dynamic parkour maneuvers, including traversing large gaps, elevated platforms, and narrow beam terrains. Under severe visual degradation, such as heavy occlusion and strong illumination changes, the robot continues to maintain stable and robust locomotion performance.

XQGBZwsuXt.a: We present a learning-based framework that enables a full-scale bipedal humanoid to sprint at over 7 m/s with motion-prior-guided gait and perform aggressive cornering at high speed with a pronounced trunk lean of up to 25◦ . Achieving this combination is challenging: above approximately 4 m/s, periodic foot impacts induce severe, high-frequency yaw-rate oscillations intrinsic to highspeed gaits. This high-frequency temporal structure corrupts the history of proprioceptive feedback that flat-MLP policies rely on, while rendering conventional yaw-rate tracking rewards counterproductive, as they fight against the robot’s natural oscillatory dynamics. Moreover, a single style prior shared across skills cannot tell which skill is commanded and inherently compromises the low-speed skill fidelity. To overcome these limitations, we adopt a causal multi-head attention (MHA) module to explicitly model the high-frequency temporal feedback. In place of the oscillatory yaw rate, we design a heading-direction reward that supervises only the low-frequency velocity direction, allowing agile turning at high speed without suppressing natural gait oscillations. We further introduce skill∗ † Equal contribution. Corresponding author. conditioned multi-adversarial-motion-prior (MAMP) discriminators that condition the style reward on the commanded skill. Ablation experiments confirm that each mechanism is essential: replacing structured temporal encoding with a flathistory MLP caps the top speed; reverting to yaw-rate tracking prevents highspeed turning; and a single shared discriminator makes in-place turning collapse into a quasi-static stance. Our framework bridges the gap between raw sprinting speed and reference-motion fidelity, demonstrating stable high-speed sprinting and aggressive cornering in both simulation and real-robot deployment (videos: https://youtu.be/YWf62XkiApc).

2tjuz95jmb.a: While current Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) provide robust control priors for humanoids, they only execute pre-defined reference motions. As a result, they are vulnerable to environmental shifts and incapable of reactive whole-body coordination. Naively cascading them with generative motion planners fails to achieve true reactivity, as inevitable tracking discrepancies induce fatal cumulative exposure bias. To bridge this gap, we propose ReactiveBFM, a real-time closed-loop planning-control framework. At its core, we effectively mitigate exposure bias via a scheduled prefix sampling curriculum, forcing the generative planner to actively learn error-recovery behaviors from imperfect physical states rather than ground-truth trajectories. Systematically, to reconcile the severe latency mismatch between auto-regressive planning and high-frequency tracking, we introduce an asynchronous replanning mechanism. Combined with trajectory chunking to temporally ensemble spatial references, our system guarantees spatio-temporally fluid execution without physical jitter. Deployed on the Unitree G1 humanoid, ReactiveBFM demonstrates unprecedented physical agility across a vast repertoire of text-conditioned closed-loop motions. Notably, ReactiveBFM achieves zero-shot moving target reaching, showcasing intricate wholebody coordination and on-the-fly replanning. In sim-to-sim benchmarking under severe perturbations, ReactiveBFM achieves a 93.1% success rate, significantly outperforming cascaded open-loop baselines by 28.6%. Our code is available at https://github.com/zjwzcx/ReactiveBFM. ∗ Core contributors (listed in random order). † Corresponding authors.

rEmMzoUnpn.a: Safe control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to their highdimensional dynamics, contact-rich interactions, and sensitivity to disturbances. Although reinforcement learning has enabled effective locomotion and motion tracking, learned policies can still generate unsafe actions that lead to instability or falls. In this work, we propose residual reinforcement learning as an implicit safety-filtering mechanism for safe humanoid control. Instead of relying on a single nominal policy to simultaneously balance performance, safety, and robustness, we decouple performance and safety. The nominal policy focuses solely on task performance, while a residual policy learns safety corrections. This decoupling leads to a better performance–safety Pareto trade-off and avoids the need for careful tuning of multiple competing reward terms within a single policy training. We show that the residual policy can act as an implicit safety filter. We evaluate our method in challenging humanoid balance tasks. Compared with the nominal reference policy and a learning-based safety filter baseline, residual reinforcement learning improves safety while still achieving competent performance.
rEmMzoUnpn.k: Humanoid Whole-body Control, Safety, Residual Reinforcement Learning, Safe Reinforcement Learning, Safety Filter

uMgOYXmgn2.a: Humanoid locomotion requires control policies that remain stable under imperfect sensing while exploiting temporal context for consistent motion. We present RoboDreamer, a two-stage teacher–student framework that combines nextobservation consistency with randomized continuous temporal masking. A teacher is first trained on clean observations, and a student is then distilled under masked recent observations, encouraging the policy to infer missing current information from history. At inference, the same masking interface is reused for implicit closed* Equal Contribution. † ‡ Project Lead. Corresponding Author. loop action refinement and optional multi-step action chunking. Mamba is used as the temporal backbone, while matched ablations show that masking/distillation provides a substantial part of the gain and Mamba contributes additional tracking improvements with real-time latency. Experiments in IsaacLab, MuJoCo, and on a Unitree G1 demonstrate robust motion tracking under observation masking and successful real-world deployment.
uMgOYXmgn2.k: Humanoid Locomotion, Temporal Reasoning, State-Space Models, Mamba Policy, Robot Learning

WBGnJHRIso.a: Elite humanoid soccer shooting requires whole-body stability, highimpulse whole-body interactions, and accuracy to targets. Motion tracking-driven reinforcement learning (RL) provides stability in whole-body movement coordination, but a fixed reference makes it hard to adapt to varied ball positions and strike timings; in contrast, task reward-driven RL struggles to explore and discover valid kicks from scratch. We therefore introduce RoboNaldo, a three-stage motionguided curriculum RL framework for high-impulse humanoid interaction. A single human-kick reference is used as a scaffold and progressively shifts optimization towards shooting performance. The curriculum first learns stable whole-body kicking prior, then adapts the kick to free-kick settings where the ball is stationary at random positions, and finally extends it to moving-ball shooting through a locomotion-command and kick-trigger interface. A high-level heuristic planner controls this interface during training, while alternative high-level controllers can drive the same low-level policy at inference. In simulation, RoboNaldo demonstrates free-kick shot error 48.6% lower and shoot velocity 2.96× than prior work baselines. In real world on a Unitree G1 with onboard perception, RoboNaldo attains 0.73 m and 0.86 m average target shooting error from 3 m away in free-kick and moving-ball cases, accordingly. And the post-contact ball velocity reaches 13.10 m/s, which is 59–71% of reported professional open-play shot speed. Project page: https://opendrivelab.com/RoboNaldo.
WBGnJHRIso.k: Athletic robots, humanoid-object interaction, sim-to-real transfer

zYpPmDICVV.a: Humanoid perceptive locomotion has made significant progress and shows great promise, yet achieving robust multi-directional locomotion on complex terrains remains underexplored. To tackle this challenge, we propose RPL, a two-stage training framework that enables multi-directional locomotion on challenging terrains, and remains robust with payloads. RPL first trains terrain-specific expert policies with privileged height map observations to master decoupled locomotion and manipulation skills across different terrains, and then distills them into a transformer policy that leverages multiple depth cameras to cover a wide range of views. During distillation, we introduce two techniques to robustify multidirectional locomotion, depth feature scaling based on velocity commands and random side masking, which are critical for asymmetric depth observations and unseen widths of terrains. For scalable depth distillation, we develop an efficient multi-depth system that ray-casts against both dynamic robot meshes and static terrain meshes in massively parallel environments, achieving a 5× speedup over the depth rendering pipelines in existing simulators while modeling realistic sensor latency, noise, and dropout. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate robust multi-directional locomotion with payloads (2 kg) across challenging terrains, including 20◦ slopes, staircases with different step lengths (22 cm, 25 cm, 30 cm), and 25 cm×25 cm stepping stones separated by 60 cm gaps.
zYpPmDICVV.k: Humanoid Perceptive Locomotion, RL, Imitation Learning

VTSUekrCnH.a: Conventional object transport typically relies on containers, fences, or tethers to secure the payload. Here, a wheel-legged robot transports up to five identical, free-rolling steel spheres on an open back plate without physical restraints. Because the spheres are indistinguishable, their observation-slot assignments may change independently across history frames, creating a per-frame permutation symmetry that standard history-concatenation set encoders do not enforce. This mismatch becomes a bottleneck beyond two spheres: under the same PPO budget, flat and branch-wise MLPs plateau at or below two spheres, while the reference unaugmented history-concatenation Deep Sets baseline (DSHC) stalls at two spheres; additional seeds eventually advance beyond two spheres, but only slowly and late in training. We introduce Per-Frame Deep Sets (PFDS), which pools objects invariantly within each frame before temporal fusion. PFDS is Gframe -invariant by construction, and we prove universal approximation of continuous Gframe -invariant policies. In a 2×2 ablation over architecture and slot randomization, PFDS reaches five spheres across all five seeds and achieves 100% no-drop transport, while augmentation improves the reliability of DSHC curriculum progression. We also distill the privileged PFDS teacher into TACT S ET, which replaces privileged object-state observations with a Gframe -invariant binary union contact map while retaining proprioceptive history, and retains 75% no-drop performance with five spheres. Finally, we run the S2M-Trek deployment stack closed-loop on a physical wheel-legged robot for every sphere count k=1, · · · , 5. The measured tactile maps contain one connected component per sphere but no persistent identity, complementing the quantitative simulation results. Demonstrations are available at drgon-li.github.io/PFDS.

rJe0dLlPev.a: Humans expand their locomotion capability by wearing appropriate footwear, such as hiking boots for mountains or skates for ice. Footwear changes the ground-contact interface and enables traversal of otherwise difficult terrain. In contrast, locomotion controllers are typically trained for a fixed morphology, and their performance can degrade when shoes alter foot geometry, mass, and friction. We propose SHOES, a sample-efficient framework for adapting locomotion policies to footwear-induced morphology changes. SHOES freezes a simulationtrained nominal policy and fine-tunes only lightweight, identity-initialized modulation modules on the robot, preserving the initial behavior while enabling efficient hardware adaptation. We also introduce SafeBox, a workspace-aware waypoint sampler that constrains online adaptation within a user-defined workspace. The simulation results with a shoe-equipped Unitree Go2 show that SHOES substantially recovers locomotion performance after footwear-induced morphology changes using limited additional adaptation. Under the same adaptation budget, SHOES outperforms FiLM-only, Linear Adapter-only, and residual-RL baselines. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 fitted with human shoes further evaluate the effectiveness of SHOES for hardware deployment.
rJe0dLlPev.k: Legged Locomotion, Online Adaptation, Sim-to-Real, FiLM, Linear Adapter, Safe Online RL

aRtb8NIgc3.a: Humanoid foundation models are advancing faster than we can evaluate them. While real-world testing is expensive and difficult to reproduce, existing simulation benchmarks focus primarily on table-top or wheeled robots. A scalable and reproducible benchmark for whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation remains an open problem. To this end, we present SIMPLE, a unified simulation testbed for humanoid policy learning and evaluation. SIMPLE couples the accurate contact-rich dynamics of MuJoCo with the photorealistic rendering of IsaacSim. It provides a large-scale environment comprising 16 diverse wholebody tasks, 50 indoor scenes, and over 1,000 object assets. To facilitate scalable data collection, the framework integrates two data generation pipelines: automated trajectory generation via motion planning and a low-latency VR teleoperation interface. We further integrate and benchmark mainstream humanoid policies at scale in SIMPLE, including lightweight imitation networks, large visionlanguage-action (VLA) models, and recent world action models (WAMs). Our experiments demonstrate that policies trained on data collected in SIMPLE can be transferred zero-shot to physical humanoid robots under similar settings, providing a robust and reproducible foundation for humanoid robotics research.
aRtb8NIgc3.k: Humanoid Loco-Manipulation, Simulation-based Evaluation, Wholebody Foundation Models

cHCwUratwL.a: Humanoid soccer is a challenging testbed for dynamic whole-body control, requiring robots to coordinate balance, locomotion, object interaction, and skill switching over long horizons. Existing humanoid sports methods often rely on taskspecific multi-stage pipelines, making it difficult to jointly learn and compose multiple object-interactive skills within a single deployable policy. To address this, we present SkillX, a unified reinforcement learning framework that learns and composes multiple atomic soccer skills through a single command-conditioned policy. SkillX integrates three core designs: skill-specific adversarial motion priors, skill-specific critics, and an object-aware temporal encoder, enabling the robot to execute atomic skills and transition among them such as dribbling, trapping, and shooting. Experiments in simulation and on a real Noetix E1 humanoid demonstrate robust multi-skill execution, long-horizon skill composition, and successful sim-to-real deployment.
cHCwUratwL.k: Humanoid Robots, Reinforcement Learning, Multi-Task Learning
