The model achieves mean trajectory prediction errors of <8% on held out tasks and users, with effectively instantaneous deterministic inference and sub-second sampling of trajectory distributions. User-specific fine-tuning further reduces error using only minutes of additional data collection and training. An initial test using the model during live rehabilitation tasks demonstrates that, on average, participants reach the target neuromotor activations with just 15% error accumulated throughout the task.
Tk20sRMzhv.k: personalized rehabilitation, sequence modeling, human–robot interaction

XKZ7YJEfr4.a: Recent advancements in learning from human demonstration have shown promising results in addressing the scalability and high cost of data collection required to train robust visuomotor policies. However, existing approaches are often constrained by a reliance on multiview camera setups, depth sensors, or custom hardware, and are typically limited to policy execution from third-person or egocentric cameras. In this paper, we present WARPED, a framework designed to synthesize realistic wrist-view observations and actions from human demonstration videos to facilitate the training of visuomotor policies using only monocular RGB data. With data collected from an egocentric RGB camera, our system leverages vision foundation models to initialize the interactive scene. A hand-object interaction pipeline is then employed to track the hand and manipulated object and retarget the trajectories to a robotic end-effector. Lastly, photorealistic wristview observations are synthesized via Gaussian Splatting to directly train a robotic policy. We demonstrate that WARPED achieves success rates comparable to teleoperation on four of five rigid-object tabletop tasks and one articulated-object task, while requiring 4-9× less data collection time.
XKZ7YJEfr4.k: Robot Manipulation, Imitation Learning, Robot Data Generation

x05Rf7L7H4.a: Imitation learning typically treats every demonstration state as equally important, optimizing a behavior-cloning objective uniformly across the dataset. Yet not all states are created equal: in a small number of critical states, even a slight deviation from the expert action can lead to a failure, while in many other states such errors are recoverable and inconsequential. We formalize state criticality in imitation learning as the worst-case degradation in downstream value induced by a bounded perturbation of the expert action at a given state. We then propose SCRIM, a practical State CRIticality Measure that estimates this quantity by training an adversarial disturbance policy and a value critic around a fixed imitation policy. SCRIM assigns each demonstration state a score reflecting how vulnerable the task outcome is to small, policy-relevant action errors. We show that these scores can be used to reweight behavior-cloning losses, improving imitation at consequential states and increasing overall task performance. We further show that SCRIM enables data curation by selecting compact, high-value subsets of demonstrations that preserve performance while substantially reducing the amount of training data. We evaluate SCRIM across various simulated and realworld robotic manipulation tasks, and demonstrate that SCRIM improves policy training, enables efficient data selection, and provides interpretable insights into which moments in a demonstration are most critical for task success. Project website: https://sia-lab-git.github.io/SCRIM/
x05Rf7L7H4.k: Data Quality, Imitation Learning, Robotic Manipulation

u56Z5KqtkI.a: Action chunking—predicting and executing multiple actions instead of a single action—has proven to be a critical component for learning effective robotic control policies. However, our precise understanding of why action chunking improves performance has remained limited. In this work we seek to close this gap. Through rigorous experimental evaluations in both simulated and real-world settings, we show that existing hypotheses for the success of action chunking—temporal consistency, horizon reduction, and representation learning—fail to explain the success of action chunking. Instead, we find that action chunking benefits from greater non-Markovian expressivity and reduced compounding error compared to Markovian policies, but, in many settings of interest, these effects can be fully captured by delayed policies, which at each step predict a single action based on the observation k steps in the past. We then show that there exists an additional benefit of action chunking that we refer to as implicit ensembling. In particular, by learning a diversity of temporal relationships (that is, at |ot , at |ot´1 , . . .), action-chunked policies exhibit behavior matching that of a model ensemble, increasing their robustness and generalization ability over policies that only learn a single temporal relationship. Building on these insights, we show that in simulated and real-world robotic control settings, we can match the performance of action chunking without action chunking—by deploying an action chunking policy as an ensemble of policies with randomized delays. Furthermore, we propose a policy class that amplifies the benefits of action chunking by explicitly instantiating an ensemble, and which we show significantly improves over the performance of action chunking in many domains. Website: https://action-chunking.github.io.

uoFfrJHHq8.a: Bidirectional thrust grants quadrotors a second equilibrium condition and increased control authority, expanding the envelope of possible aggressive maneuvers and enabling inverted flight, perching, and sensing. Prior geometric control approaches extend differential flatness through Hopf fibration-based attitude representations to support bidirectional thrust, but struggle with actuator saturation and motor reversal delay during inversions, requiring heuristic thrust posture scheduling and waypoint tuning. We propose a learning-based framework that modulates a constant reference trajectory to perform compact, positionconstrained quadrotor inversions while remaining compatible with traditional trajectory generation and tracking across flight regimes. Separate policies are trained via reinforcement learning for nominal-to-inverted and inverted-to-nominal transitions. In JAX-based simulation, the proposed method achieves the lowest position deviation and settling time across all evaluated baselines, reducing position root mean square error (RMSE) and settling time by at least 25% and 39%, respectively, relative to the strongest optimization-based baseline. Hardware experiments demonstrate successful inversion across multiple yaw configurations with position RMSE below 0.33 m, and compatibility with downstream trajectory generation and control through circular flight in both regimes. Additionally, we provide a project website1 with additional experiment videos and an open-source implementation of the proposed framework2 .
uoFfrJHHq8.k: Reinforcement Learning, Geometric Control, Aerial Robotics

xyRbF93MWh.a: Safe navigation in dynamic environments requires robots to plan under obstacle predictions whose errors are uncertain, non-stationary, and can induce rare but safety-critical failures. Existing control-barrier-function safety filters can reject immediately unsafe controls, but they provide little guidance on when the current finite-horizon planning mode itself is becoming unsafe as prediction uncertainty evolves. We propose Conformal Event-Triggered Risk-Certified Replanning (CERT-Replan), a framework that uses calibrated barrier risk as an early-warning signal for replanning. CERT-Replan calibrates horizon-indexed obstacle-prediction residuals online and uses the resulting uncertainty radii to evaluate dynamic-obstacle safety margins. A one-step safety filter protects the next applied control, while a horizon-level risk monitor evaluates the upper-tail CVaR of predicted barrier-violation losses along the current MPC rollout. When this risk exceeds an allocated budget, CERT-Replan rejects the current planning mode and selects a lower-risk alternative, such as a different speed profile, corridor, or homotopy class, rather than repeatedly correcting the same nominal plan. In a non-stationary benchmark, CERT-Replan achieves an 83.3% collision reduction relative to the safety-filter-only baseline and a 77.8% reduction relative to simple replanning triggers, while reducing average safety-filter intervention by 32.4%. With Trajectron++, CERT-Replan achieves 96% collision-free operation. Hardware experiments and onboard runtime profiling demonstrate computational feasibility.
xyRbF93MWh.k: Mobile Robot Navigation, Event-Triggered Replanning, Conformal Prediction, Risk-Aware Safety, Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance

8iFziu27Yy.a: Standardized benchmarks have played a central role in advancing robot manipulation learning, yet most focus on ground-supported manipulation systems, which limits their applicability to dynamics-critical domains such as aerial manipulation (AM). AM presents distinct system-level challenges, including environmental disturbances, coupled dynamics between the manipulator and floating base, and constrained degrees of freedom. Consequently, task performance depends jointly on robot embodiment, low-level control, and high-level policy design. We introduce AM-Bench, a modular simulation suite and benchmark for multirotor-based AM policy learning. AM-Bench includes representative embodiments spanning underactuated, fully actuated, and overactuated systems, 12 tasks across contact, transport, and constrained interaction, configurable aerodynamic disturbances and actuator saturation, standard low-level controllers, and baseline policy-learning algorithms. Unlike prior manipulation benchmarks that primarily emphasize end-to-end policy performance, AM-Bench enables system-level evaluation of how embodiment, control, disturbances, and policy choices interact. We demonstrate its diagnostic value through three simulation studies spanning highlevel policies, policy–control interfaces, and embodiments, together with realworld validation of modeled effects and a hardware test of the learning pipeline. The project website is https://ambench.github.io/.
8iFziu27Yy.k: Benchmarks and datasets for robot learning, Robot manipulation, Aerial robots

eGZ6YMFVzU.a: Anomaly detection is essential for ensuring the safety and reliability of autonomous driving systems operating in open environments, where rare objects, abnormal behaviors, and long-tail events frequently arise. Conventional perception-based approaches often lack the contextual understanding necessary to interpret complex anomalies, while recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods incur substantial computational overhead and exhibit limited integration with geometric sensory modalities. To address these challenges, we propose SOFA, an adaptive slow-fast anomaly detection and reasoning framework that selectively activates multimodal reasoning only when anomalous events are detected. SOFA integrates three key components: 1) a fast LiDAR-based anomaly detection module for efficient real-time perception, 2) a slow VLM-based reasoning module for semantic understanding, and 3) a Time-to-Collision (TTC)-driven switching mechanism that dynamically coordinates the two modules to balance efficiency and reasoning fidelity. To enable systematic evaluation of multimodal anomaly detection and reasoning in real-world driving scenarios, we further construct MAQA, a Multimodal Anomaly Question Answering dataset comprising 16K anomalous objects, synchronized LiDAR-image observations, and reasoning-oriented language annotations. Extensive experiments on MAQA demonstrate that SOFA significantly outperforms baselines in detection accuracy, computational efficiency, and reasoning capability. The code is released at: https://github.com/ZY-Zong/ Adaptive-Slow-fast-Anomaly-Detection-and-Reasoning
eGZ6YMFVzU.k: Slow-Fast Framework, Anomaly Detection and Reasoning, Autonomous Driving

j5QcZcRrda.a: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and low latency, making them ideal sensors for high-speed robotic applications where conventional cameras suffer from motion blur. However, their widespread adoption in robot learning is severely bottlenecked by the computational cost of simulating highfrequency event data during online training. In this work, we present Approximate Imitation Learning, a novel framework that fundamentally resolves this bottleneck, reducing policy training time for complex, agile drone flight from 52.44 hours to just 1.86 hours—a 28× computational speedup. Our key insight is to separate representation learning from policy search. We first leverage a largescale offline dataset to learn a task-specific representation space. Subsequently, the policy is fine-tuned through online interactions that rely solely on lightweight state information, completely eliminating the need to render events during the active policy search phase. This training paradigm drastically reduces development overhead and enables event-based control policies to scale to complex environments. Furthermore, our approach eliminates the reliance on standard cameras or intermediate representations during deployment, mapping events directly to control commands. In simulation, our method matches or exceeds the performance of standard imitation learning baselines that require full online event rendering. Finally, we successfully validate the framework in the real world, demonstrating that a policy trained via this ultra-efficient paradigm enables a quadrotor to fly through highly cluttered environments at remarkable speeds of up to 9.8 ms−1 .

2LNbCnzTQk.a: Embodied agents are typically built as hand-designed compositions of perception, memory, planning, and action modules. This modularity exposes a large architectural design space, but current systems still rely on researcher intuition to choose where information is stored, how observations are processed, and how model calls are connected. Agent Architecture Search (AAS) automates such design for text-domain agents, but has not been systematically evaluated on perceptual embodied agents. We study this transfer. To make embodied architectures searchable, we introduce AGENT C ANVAS on the executor side, representing embodied agents as editable typed graphs with simulator execution and episodelevel logs. On the optimizer side, we lift AAS from LLM-call loops to toolusing coding-agent sessions, adapting ADAS and AFlow and introducing Knowledge Distill Loop (KDLoop). Across four embodied executors (MapGPT, SmartWay, ExploreEQA, and VoxPoser), search discovers improvements that persist on episodes never queried during search. KDLoop and AFlow independently discover elevation-tolerant observation processing. KDLoop’s implementation also improves success rates over the baseline when transferred to real robots. These improvements are not uniform: some gains remain uncertain or reverse on heldout episodes, and an apparent gain exploits evaluator-side information. The experiments further show how rollout noise, local edit basins, and incomplete use of episode-level evidence constrain search. Together, these results establish the potential of automated architecture search for embodied agents and characterize the challenges of applying it in simulated and real-world environments. Code is available at https://github.com/jianzhou0420/AgentCanvas.
2LNbCnzTQk.k: Embodied Agents, Agent Architecture Search, LLM Agents

YnMZwXZ68A.a: Open-loop (OL) to closed-loop (CL) gap (OL-CL gap) exists when OL-pretrained policies scoring high in OL evaluations fail to transfer effectively in closed-loop (CL) deployment. In this paper, we unveil the root causes of this systemic failure and propose a practical remedy. Specifically, we demonstrate that OL policies suffer from Observational Domain Shift and Objective Mismatch. We show that while the former is largely recoverable with adaptation techniques, the latter creates a structural inability to model complex reactive behaviors, which forms the primary OL-CL gap. We find that a wide range of OL policies learn a biased Q-value estimator that neglects both the reactive nature of CL simulations and the temporal awareness needed to reduce compounding errors. To this end, we propose a Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) framework that calibrates observational shift, reduces state-action biases, and enforces temporal consistency. Extensive experiments show that TTA effectively mitigates planning biases and yields superior scaling dynamics than its baseline counterparts. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the existence of blind spots in standard OL evaluation protocols that fail to capture the realities of closed-loop deployment.
YnMZwXZ68A.k: Autonomous Driving, Closed-loop Simulation, Test-time Adaptation

Hi8mV09nOi.a: Vision-Language Navigation has increasingly emphasized high-level instruction reasoning, memory, global map construction, and instruction decomposition, while the low-level action representation remains comparatively underexplored. We propose CoFL-S, a low-level vision-language-action framework that predicts a language-conditioned flow field over the robot’s local visible sector and generates continuous trajectories by rolling out the predicted field. To train this low-level representation, we convert each VLN-CE episode, originally a whole-episode instruction paired with an action sequence, into frame-level local supervision with aligned sub-instructions and matched action, trajectory, and dense flow-field targets. For evaluation, we introduce a continuous-time Habitat benchmark that isolates low-level action interfaces from instruction decomposition and executes all methods through a shared velocity-command controller, enabling decomposition-independent closed-loop comparison across different planner frequencies rather than fixed discrete forward-and-turn transitions in VLNCE. Under matched encoders and training settings, CoFL-S consistently outperforms baselines across planner frequencies in the continuous-time Habitat benchmark, and zero-shot real-world closed-loop deployment further shows its advantage over the evaluated baselines beyond simulation. See the project website at: https://github.com/ut-dragon-lab/CoFL.
Hi8mV09nOi.k: Action Representation, Flow-Field Policies, Vision-Language Navigation

xm8LPYlbxA.a: Robots are often deployed in environments where safety must be learned from experience rather than specified in advance. Demonstrations, operator interventions, near misses, and failed rollouts can reveal which behaviors are risky, but they provide only local evidence. The key challenge is not only to identify risky behavior, but to make that knowledge shape the distance used for long-horizon planning. Existing goal-conditioned methods can compose shorthorizon behaviors into longer plans, but they typically assume that the relevant cost structure is already known. We introduce CoGeL, a constraint-to-geometry learning method that learns a soft safety signal from robot data and incorporates it directly into the goal-reaching distance used for planning. This makes the learned distance safety-aware rather than treating safety as a separate classifier, hard mask, or post-hoc filter. We show that errors in the learned safety signal induce bounded changes in the navigation geometry, that route consistency supports composition through intermediate waypoints, and that, under a calibration condition, the learned safety scores bound the expected number of safety violations. Experiments across wheeled and legged navigation tasks show that CoGeL reduces unsafe events while maintaining strong long-horizon goal-reaching performance. Project Page: https://pralgomathic.github.io/cogel/
xm8LPYlbxA.k: Robot Learning, Long-Horizon Navigation, Constraint-to-Geometry Learning, Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning, Quasimetric Learning

lSrxDURLdG.a: Collaborative planning under operational constraints is essential for heterogeneous robot teams in large-scale missions. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) provide rapid area coverage but are limited by onboard energy, while Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) can serve as mobile recharging stations yet are constrained by road-network traversability. Effective collaboration must enforce operational constraints during execution while enabling parallel, coordinated actions. Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) have shown promise through token unmasking but have two key limitations: entropy-guided scheduling assumes distributional alignment and reliance on differentiable constraints for diffusion-time optimization. We propose Masked Error-bounded Neuro-Symbolic Diffusion (MEND), which formulates collaborative planning as a conditional masked generative process to generate context-aware action sequences for UAV-UGV teams. MEND introduces a neuro-symbolic diffusion paradigm that constrains conditional masked diffusion policies at execution by reweighting the learned action distribution with a logicinduced admissibility indicator, thereby enforcing compliance with operational constraints. MEND introduces an error-bounded inference scheduling at execution that constructs the unmasking schedule by selecting positions with minimal predictive entropy over the constraint-aware action distribution, enhancing collaborative planning optimality under operational constraints. Extensive experimental results in simulation, on real-world maps, and with physical robot teams demonstrate that MEND advances UAV-UGV collaborative planning under operational constraints. More details are available on the website: https://hcrlab.gitlab.io/project/mend.

v4QUDwGroQ.a: Robots are increasingly expected to provide personalized services in everyday environments. To do so, they must ground natural-language commands such as Where is my backpack? or Find my bottle and execute them by reasoning about object instances, people, locations, and ownership. This is challenging because ownership is rarely labeled explicitly and must be inferred from long-term, behavioral evidence of human–object interactions. To address this, we present COOL, a novel robotic framework for autonomously learning object ownership from everyday observations and maintaining a long-term spatial memory of its environment. To keep its memory current, COOL uses an agent-based curiositydriven data collection strategy that guides the robot toward the most promising locations to gain information and refresh stale observations. Offline experiments, ablation studies, and real-world evaluations show that COOL can infer ownership relations from real-world interactions and use this knowledge for ownershipconditioned navigation and task execution. Code, prompts, and evaluation data are available at: https://samirahuber.github.io/cool.
v4QUDwGroQ.k: Spatial Memory, Object Ownership, Robotic Assistance

da5VPQA7G7.a: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes. Our code and videos are available at https://coopuq.github.io/.
da5VPQA7G7.k: Social Navigation, Multi-Robot Systems, Occupancy Forecasting

ojMvvFKk6t.a: Feature matching underpins many robotic perception tasks, including visual localization, mapping, SLAM, and autonomous navigation. Existing semi-dense matchers predict confidence on fixed grids, limiting correspondences to predefined locations and requiring costly high-resolution grids for precise localization. We present CoReMatch (Coordinate Refinement Match), a recurrent framework that refines correspondences directly in continuous coordinate space rather than predicting discrete confidence maps. CoReMatch progressively improves correspondence estimates by propagating information across iterations. At the coarse stage, a Deep Aggregated Transformer captures global context and iteratively updates correspondence coordinates, while a lightweight regression head further sharpens their localization. Experiments on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show that CoReMatch strikes a strong balance between accuracy and efficiency, outperforming Efficient LoFTR in accuracy while running more than 10× faster on embedded edge hardware. These results demonstrate that recurrent coordinate refinement offers an efficient and scalable approach to real-time feature matching for robotic perception. Code is available at edge-cv/CoReMatch.
ojMvvFKk6t.k: Feature Matching, Robotic Perception, Iterative Refinement

pTqOGquuCh.a: Safe autonomous navigation requires not only geometric obstacle avoidance but also semantic awareness. Different object categories demand different safety clearances, and the set of relevant categories may expand as the robot explores novel environments. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer rich semantic representations for building maps of unknown scenes, yet their confidence scores are poorly calibrated, making raw predictions unreliable for safetycritical planning. Conformal prediction (CP) can provide coverage guarantees, but existing methods assume a fixed label set and stationary data, limiting their use in open-world settings. We propose Conformal Semantic Mapping for OpenWorld Safe Robot Navigation (CoSMO), a semantic safety mapping framework that transforms VLM embeddings into calibrated coverage sets and safety-aware obstacle dilations over a dynamically expanding hazard vocabulary, even under distribution shift. Experiments on the Matterport3D (MP3D) dataset show that CoSMO reduces semantic collisions by 61.6% relative to a geometry-only baseline, while maintaining formal coverage guarantees even under delayed expert feedback. Real-world experiments on a quadruped robot further demonstrate generalization by achieving long-run empirical coverage of 90.73% against the 90% target. Project website: https://yangming911.github.io/cosmo-page/.
pTqOGquuCh.k: Robot Navigation, Robot Safety, Formal Guarantees, Conformal Prediction

qbninLImrj.a: Current navigation benchmarks focus on task success but do not capture the economic constraints essential for commercializing autonomous delivery systems. We introduce CostNav, an Economic Navigation Benchmark that evaluates physical AI agents on a cost-revenue and break-even analysis, pairing Isaac Sim’s collision and cargo dynamics with industry-standard data such as Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings and Abbreviated Injury Scale (AIS) injury reports. To our knowledge, CostNav is the first physics-grounded economic benchmark to use regulatory and financial data to quantify the gap between navigation metrics and commercial deployment, revealing that high task-success rates alone do not ensure economic viability. Evaluating seven baselines (two rule-based and five imitation-learning methods), we find no method economically viable: all yield negative contribution margins. CANVAS, using only an RGB camera and GPS, attains the highest task success and the least-negative margin among methods with non-zero Service-Level Agreement (SLA) compliance (−$28.40/run), outperforming LiDAR-equipped Nav2 w/ GPS (−$37.34/run). A sim-trained policy evaluated on a real delivery robot yields SLA compliance close to its simulation result, indicating that task-level SLA behavior in CostNav’s simulation transfers to physical hardware. We challenge the community to achieve economic viability on CostNav, which scores methods by cost-revenue outcomes. All resources are available at https://github.com/worv-ai/CostNav.
qbninLImrj.k: Economic Cost, Navigation Benchmark, Physical AI, Isaac Sim

LqUR3gxKdH.a: Faithfully evaluating end-to-end driving policies in simulation requires observations that are not merely photo-realistic, but preserve the scene features a policy relies on to make decisions. Existing platforms, however, exhibit a simto-real visual gap that corrupts policy perception, undermining their ability to assess a policy’s closed-loop decision-making. To this end, we propose DreamStream, a generative, closed-loop simulator that achieves policy-oriented fidelity using a simulator-grounded autoregressive video model. Our video model is distilled from a large pretrained video model via traffic layout guidance, varying visual appearance while preserving policy-relevant features such as scenario layout and the temporal consistency of dynamic objects. We further observe that perceptual metrics like FID misrank how well these features are preserved. To tackle this, we introduce FDπ, a new multi-representation metric that measures the sim-to-real gap as the Fréchet distance over scene-context features from public E2E policies. Under FDπ, DreamStream improves over the strongest prior closed-loop simulator by 1.6× on nuScenes and 4.7× on NAVSIM, and induces the least perturbation to policy’s perceptual observability. Based on DreamStream, we construct Navhard-CL benchmark, which turns non-reactive realworld benchmark NAVSIM into interactive testing environments with adversarial driving behaviors and weather variations. This benchmark exposes many failure modes of driving policies, such as scorer bias and lack of recovery behaviors, that prior closed-loop benchmarks overlook. Code and data are available at https://github.com/VAIL-UCLA/DreamStream.
LqUR3gxKdH.k: Autonomous Driving, Video Model, Closed-loop Simulation

9ccdcInkM9.a: Learning motion planning policies that remain reliable under closedloop execution is a central challenge in Autonomous Driving (AD). Imitation Learning (IL) scales well to large AD datasets but suffers from distribution shift, causal confusion, and compounding errors under closed-loop execution. In contrast, Reinforcement Learning (RL) typically requires handcrafted rule-based rewards and massive simulation. We study a simple closed-loop IL framework that uses RL purely as an optimization tool, guided by a trajectory-distance reward derived from logged expert data. We refer to this training strategy as Expert-Guided RL (EGRL). Through a controlled empirical study we find evidence that the training procedure, rather than model size and complexity, accounts for a substantial part of the performance gains. We then introduce DriveMLP, a lightweight MLP policy trained with EGRL, as a simple instantiation of these findings. It achieves a score of 86.51 on the nuPlan Val14 Reactive benchmark, a +3.2 point improvement over the previous best IL planner (Flow Planner), with > 15× faster inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/alessandro-canevaro/ DriveMLP.

fHzDEYENPF.a: Accurate and interpretable motion prediction for heterogeneous traffic spaces, including pedestrians, bicycles, cars, and trucks, is essential for safe autonomous navigation. Nevertheless, state-of-the-art approaches remain predominantly black-box, lacking explicit encoding of the regulatory and behavioral constraints of real-world mobility. We propose Trajectory Compliance-Shaping (TraCS), a neuro-symbolic framework that augments existing black-box motion prediction backbones with interpretable and probabilistic first-order logic. To do so, TraCS employs an agentic code-generation pipeline to bridge the gap between natural-language descriptions of traffic regulations and probabilistic motion prediction. Furthermore, TraCS employs a reactive data-streaming inference engine that maintains and efficiently updates compliance landscapes as scenes evolve. To prevent TraCS from overconfidently steering the backbone’s predictions in the wrong direction, we propose a neural confidence rating learned as a context-aware attenuation of the compliance signal. We demonstrate on the Argoverse 2 benchmark how TraCS consistently improves state-of-the-art prediction backbones, showing that probabilistic and symbolic compliance reasoning is a broadly applicable and computationally efficient complement to purely neural motion predictors.

dkaxE3v6uu.a: Autonomous long-horizon sidewalk navigation is essential for micromobility applications such as robotic food delivery and assistive electronic wheelchairs. Unlike autonomous driving on the road, long-horizon sidewalk navigation requires precise maneuvering through unpredictable sidewalk terrains and pedestrians, with a lightweight perception stack as minimal as a single monocular RGB camera. While imitation learning (IL) from demonstrations offers a practical solution, the resulting autopilot policy often suffers from compounding errors and struggle to make reliable progress while respecting sidewalk boundaries in complex environments. To address these challenges, we introduce FlowPilot, a mapless navigation policy that achieves robust and efficient long-horizon navigation performance using only a monocular RGB camera. We propose to use anchored flow matching as an action representation for policy pre-training on large-scale robot fleet data and to capture the diverse, complex, multimodal distribution of sidewalk navigation behaviors. To bridge the gap between imitation and alignment, we further design a human-in-the-loop preference learning scheme to tune the policy on a small amount of human intervention data. It strengthens the model’s counterfactual reasoning and social compliance on sidewalks. We evaluate FlowPilot through simulation and real-world experiments in diverse sidewalk environments. FlowPilot-Base achieves 42% success rate and 66% route completion in simulation, while FlowPilot-HP further improves robustness and social compliance, reducing IR by 40.0% and NIR by 52.1% relative to the base model.
dkaxE3v6uu.k: Visual Navigation; Imitation Learning; AI Alignment

RwGNm8fUxX.a: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) agents may satisfy conventional success criteria while still failing to establish reliable object-level grounding, because current evaluation protocols mainly reward stopping within a 3meter radius and largely ignore the agent’s final orientation and target visibility. We formalize this limitation as the Last-3-Meter Grounding Gap and introduce three instance-centric metrics to quantify proximity precision, target visibility, and final-view grounding. To mitigate this gap, we propose REALM (Regionto-Entity Alignment for Last-3-Meter Navigation), a plug-and-play, architectureagnostic refinement module that decouples fine-grained target approaching from long-horizon navigation. REALM uses a visibility-aware stopping strategy to reduce premature termination and improve final viewpoint alignment. We further construct REVERIE-AIM, which provides object-instance-level goals and 180K short-horizon training samples for final-stage target approaching. Extensive evaluations across four diverse VLN backbones show that REALM consistently improves proximity precision and visual grounding success, demonstrating its broad applicability.

m94Acp7Al5.a: UAV target following in cluttered environments requires anticipating target motion. Followers that use only the current target state can lag behind turns or choose blocked corridors. They may also trade safe near-horizon motion for lower tracking error. We propose a future-aware flow planning framework for state-informed UAV target following. Predicted target futures guide clean UAV trajectory generation through residual signals aligned with the planning horizon. Risk-scored repair of the executable prefix is embedded in the sampling loop. On fixed in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) receding-horizon benchmarks, the planner improves the safety–tracking trade-off. It matches zero measured ID collision rate and achieves the highest ID safe-tracking time fraction. It also gives the lowest OOD macro-average collision rate and final tracking error among the compared methods. It does not dominate every metric: FutureMPC remains smoother and stronger on some threshold-based OOD success metrics under its hand-designed objective. Controlled comparisons show that future conditioning with the adapter improves candidate generation before safety repair. Simulator-facing tests examine interface perturbations, sensing, and controller execution. These results support horizon-aligned future guidance and embedded prefix repair as complementary components for safe UAV target following under the tested simulation conditions.
m94Acp7Al5.k: UAV Path Planning, Future-Aware Flow Planner, Safe Trajectory Generation

1zWj66605w.a: Social navigation requires the robot to reason and respond in complex real-world environments. While recent works attempt to incorporate human-level intelligence into robot planning using large Vision-Language Models (VLMs), end-to-end frameworks often create an unpredictable black-box, and existing instruction-following methods are not designed for full autonomy. To bridge this gap, we present G2-Nav, a novel framework that grounds abstract social reasoning and guards safe real-world deployment. Instead of asking the VLM for direct planning decisions, G2-Nav translates its semantic reasoning into a vision-language costmap with reliability and interpretability. The VLM evaluates traversable regions and social agents from open-set perception, mapping social context into the costmap. To improve real-world robustness, the VLM performs semantic verification on upstream tracking, and we introduce a high-frequency safety check to guard against system latency prior to trajectory generation. We demonstrate through real-world experiments that G2-Nav delivers safe, efficient, and socially compliant autonomous navigation in unstructured environments. Code is available at https://github.com/centiLinda/G2-Nav.

EWEKI0rF6v.a: Autonomous driving requires both safe and efficient planning decisions in dynamic 3D environments. Although recent Vision/Video-Action models learn policies directly from visual observations and scale well with advances in vision transformers and large-scale training data, they often lack explicit geometric grounding and future-aware spatial guidance, limiting their ability to balance collision avoidance and driving progress. In this work, we propose GeoWorldAD, a geometry world action model that grounds trajectory planning in ego-aligned 3D space and anticipates short-horizon scene evolution with latent future geometry tokens. Present geometry provides essential spatial constraints for safe planning, while future geometry reveals how surrounding agents and ego-centric free space may evolve, reducing overly conservative decisions without sacrificing safety. To efficiently exploit these geometric cues, GeoWorldAD progressively aggregates multi-scale present geometry and latent future geometry through iterative trajectory refinement. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, highlighting the effectiveness of explicit 3D geometry grounding and future geometry world modeling for safe and efficient autonomous driving.
EWEKI0rF6v.k: Autonomous Driving, Geometry Reconstruction, World Action Model

XjyM9If1Tm.a: We propose GeoXel, a novel framework for geo-referenced 3D reconstruction from long-duration aerial video. While recent feed-forward reconstruction models have demonstrated impressive efficiency in regressing camera trajectory and 3D geometry, they suffer from two critical limitations: cumulative trajectory drift and the lack of alignment with global geographic coordinates. To address these challenges, we exploit widely accessible geo-referenced geographic data— specifically Digital Orthophoto Maps (DOM), Digital Elevation Models (DEM), and OpenStreetMap (OSM)—as a spatial grounding for precise geo-aligned reconstruction. Specifically, our method decomposes long-sequence videos into overlapping chunks and employs a transformer-based visual geometry model to capture camera trajectory and points map. We then select anchor frames from each video chunk and establish accurate correspondences and geometric transfor∗ Corresponding author. mation constraints between anchor frames and geo-referenced maps to bridge visual reconstruction results and global geographic space. A key contribution of our work is the introduction of a tailored Test-Time Training (TTT) strategy. By finetuning a sparse, carefully selected subset of the model’s layers, we successfully align the latent tokens with the geographic coordinate system. Our findings reveal that this TTT effectively preserves the reconstructed structural integrity while correcting spatial drift. Furthermore, we conduct intra-chunk and global pose graph optimization (PGO) to ensure local and global spatial consistency. Extensive evaluations on three aerial reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms existing feed-forward reconstruction baselines by a large magnitude. The project is available at https://nudt-sawlab.github.io/GeoXel/.

nl8iBTm3Mt.a: Neural inertial odometry increasingly uses networks as learned measurements inside filtering pipelines. Such measurements should transform consistently under arbitrary IMU mounting conventions: their mean must transform as a vector, and their covariance must transform congruently as a second-order tensor. We present GINIO, a geometric SO(3)-equivariant interface for neural inertial odometry under arbitrary rotations of the IMU measurement frame. Given calibrated IMU windows, our framework predicts a motion measurement and uncertainty obeying these tensorial laws. To support efficient sensor-frame learning, we introduce Last-Frame Alignment (LFA), a deterministic preprocessing step that is provably equivalent to world-frame training for SO(3)-equivariant predictors. The connected estimator tracks sensor-local states such as IMU bias, separating nuisance estimation from the geometric law enforced by the learned measurement. We instantiate the same interface in filter-connected NIO, AirIO-style recurrent aerial prediction, EqNIO-style full-SO(3) canonicalization, and ResNet-style temporal backbones. On TLIO, GINIO achieves 2.018 m ID/SO(3) ATE while EqNIO degrades to 76.389 m, using 11.6× fewer FLOPs. On NanoBench, our AirIO-style instantiation improves ATE from 5.579 m to 1.430 m without external attitude input, and our ResNet-style instantiation reaches 0.581 m ATE versus 0.645 m for ResNet1D. On Fetch, GINIO empirically reduces unseen physicalremount ATE from 8.15 m to 0.50 m without retraining, demonstrating robustness beyond the exact coordinate-frame guarantee. For uncertainty, spectral covariance reduces covariance-equivariance error by over three orders of magnitude compared with a diagonal head. Code: https://github.com/chankyo123/ginio
nl8iBTm3Mt.k: Equivariant Learning, State Estimation, Learned Inertial Odometry

xyFvvMLQRo.a: Autonomous navigation in real-world environments often requires long-horizon operation under partial observability and evolving goals. Existing mapless navigation approaches predominantly assume fixed goals throughout an episode, limiting applicability to practical scenarios where goals change online during execution. We study online chained-goal navigation, where goals evolve through existing-goal redirection or new-goal emergence without explicit transition signals. Under this setting, we find navigation may require either continued exploration or strategic revisitation, creating conflicting memory requirements. We propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (GLST), a memorydecomposition framework that separates latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations for long-horizon reasoning. We further introduce goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation under evolving goals. Extensive experiments in simulation across diverse terrains demonstrate improved chained-goal navigation performance over baselines. Realrobot experiments using the Spot quadruped further validate our memory decomposition framework.
xyFvvMLQRo.k: Online Chained-Goal Navigation, Spatio-Temporal Memory Decomposition, Reinforcement Learning

7tCsPSbYZb.a: Visual navigation has made substantial progress in learning goalreaching policies from egocentric observations. Most existing approaches primarily focus on geometric traversability, however, they do not explicitly account for the social constraints induced by human-populated environments where collisionfree space can still be socially occupied, such as the space between walking partners or within conversational formations. To address this, we present GRACE, a group-aware framework for socially compliant visual navigation. The key insight of GRACE is to explicitly model social relations and group interaction spaces, allowing the robot to avoid paths that are physically feasible but socially undesirable. Specifically, our social perception module builds a visual pedestrian– robot graph from RGB observations and uses soft F-formation targets to supervise group-aware attention. This social representation guides a visual trajectory generator, which we further finetune using group-relative reward-weighted flow matching to preserve personal and group spaces. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 demonstrate that GRACE significantly reduces group-space intrusions and collision events compared with representative baselines, while maintaining competitive navigation efficiency.

LOvZujpKxN.a: Self-play reinforcement learning has recently emerged as a way to train driving policies without any human data. It uses cheap, large-scale simulations to substitute expensive, large-scale human driving demonstrations. A key limitation of this approach is that policies trained through pure self-play can learn effective but alien driving conventions incompatible with people. Previous works attempt to mitigate such behavioral misalignments through extensive reward engineering and domain randomization, which are brittle and labor-intensive. Instead of completely discarding human demonstrations, our method treats them as a regularization objective on top of a minimal safe goal-reaching reward. Like the spice in a good stew, we find that a little human data goes a long way: our method uses only 30 minutes of human demonstrations, 2500× fewer than comparable imitation learning approaches. Resulting policies coordinate with held-out human trajectories and complete training in 15 hours on a single consumer-grade GPU. Videos and source code are available at https://spiced-self-play.com/.
LOvZujpKxN.k: Self-play Reinforcement Learning, Imitation Learning, Autonomous Driving

6RJsxVCnhB.a: Object navigation requires a robot to search for an unobserved target in an unknown environment by deciding where to explore next under partial observability. Effective search resembles human-like exploration: selectively probing visually promising frontiers while relying on spatial memory to avoid redundant revisits. We propose IntentNav, a spatial-visual imitation framework that learns human-like ObjectNav policies from human demonstrations. To infer high-level search intent from low-level human actions, we introduce Frontier-based HumanIntent Labeling, which looks ahead in human demonstrations and labels the frontier that best explains the demonstrator’s future search direction. We construct a spatial-visual candidate space, where BEV memory tracks explored regions, unexplored frontiers, and trajectory history, while egocentric visual memory provides semantic cues for each candidate. A VLM policy is trained to select among these grounded candidates, using Intent-Aligned Objective to encourage consistent and human-like exploration. IntentNav achieves state-of-the-art performance among learning-based methods on the MP3D, HM3D-v1, and HM3D-v2 ObjectNav benchmarks, attaining the best success rate among all compared methods. The proposed candidate-level navigation interface transfers zero-shot to wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid robots without further VLM fine-tuning. Project page.
6RJsxVCnhB.k: Object Navigation, Vision-Language Models, Imitation Learning

CKVUqG4YQf.a: Recent advances in vision language action (VLA) models have shown remarkable potential for autonomous driving by directly mapping multimodal inputs to control signals. However, previous VLA-based methods have not explicitly exploited the critic capability of VLAs to refine driving decisions, even though such capability has been well demonstrated in other LLM-based domains, thereby limiting their performance in complex closed-loop scenarios. In this work, we present a theoretically inspired two-stage framework, CriticVLA, which extends the role of VLAs from acting to judging. CriticVLA first generates a rough trajectory and then refines it through multimodal evaluation and single-step optimization guided by a VLA-based critic, yielding higher-quality driving behaviors. To support this process, we construct a large-scale synthetic dataset of 12.9 million annotated trajectories covering diverse driving scenarios, which enhances the critic’s reasoning and refinement abilities. Extensive closed-loop experiments on the Bench2Drive benchmark show that CriticVLA significantly surpasses baselines, achieving a 73.33% total success rate and delivering about 30% improvement in challenging scenarios.
CKVUqG4YQf.k: Autonomous Driving, Vision Language Action (VLA) models

Av4ykyMvpX.a: We propose LCLA (Language-Conditioned Latent Alignment), a framework for vision-language navigation that decouples perception from control by aligning visual-language observations to the latent representation of a frozen privileged expert policy. A lightweight adapter maps frozen vision-language embeddings into the expert latent space using supervised latent alignment rather than end-to-end policy optimization, enabling expert navigation behavior to be reused across perception backbones and environmental variations. We evaluate LCLA across in-distribution simulation, zero-shot out-of-distribution environments, robustness perturbations, and direct real-world deployment on a TurtleBot platform, where it improves OOD success rate from 49.3% to 80.5% and reduces collision rates from 45.0% to 15.5% relative to direct behavior cloning. Without any realworld fine-tuning or calibration, LCLA attains 70.7% real-world success, compared to 60.9% for a navigation-pretrained baseline and 40.2% for direct behavior cloning, demonstrating robust and efficient sim2real transfer while remaining lightweight at inference time.

n0v95NpvyY.a: Quadrotor pursuit-evasion in cluttered environments requires the pursuer to jointly track the evader and avoid obstacles. Policies trained with local distance or visibility rewards can become short-sighted: actions that reduce the current distance may still lead to blocked routes, unsafe maneuvers, or states with poor future capture feasibility. We propose a differentiable framework that trains non-myopic pursuit policies through closed-loop rollouts. Specifically, we introduce Global Reachability Value (GRV), a training-only value that evaluates future capture potential, guiding the policy toward obstacle-aware states that facilitate long-term success. Furthermore, to handle intermittent target observations, we introduce the Visibility-Gated Residual Belief (VGRB). This mechanism maintains target state estimation by coupling a Kalman motion prior with a visibility-gated residual predictor. In simulation validation, the proposed framework achieves 89.65%, 86.52%, and 76.04% capture rates with zero collisions in three representative cluttered scenarios. Ablations show that GRV reduces myopic route-selection failures, while VGRB improves target-state estimation under occlusion. Experiments in Gazebo and the real world further validate the effectiveness of our framework.
n0v95NpvyY.k: Aerial Robotics, Pursuit-evasion, Occlusion, Target Belief, Differentiable Physics

NWlhQeCX3L.a: Threading a quadrotor through a moving narrow gap is a demanding test of agile flight, requiring centimeter-level spatial alignment and precise temporal execution. We address this challenge using a control policy that operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands. The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision. Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open. We introduce a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane, turning a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective. We integrate this formulation into a visual-feature-to-command policy trained in one stage from random initialization, without a teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments. In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a 99.3% success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU. Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80% success rate over 10 physical trials. Å Video: https://youtu.be/z-txORkhnrg § Code: https://github.com/uzh-rpg/agile_narrow_gap_diffsim
NWlhQeCX3L.k: Visuomotor Policy, Differentiable Simulation, Agile Quadrotor Flight

bqXyS2gKba.a: End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models achieve strong planning performance but remain largely opaque, limiting observability and trust. We apply mechanistic interpretability to E2E driving by training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on the internal activations of a simple, single-camera end-to-end path planning model. Unsupervised clustering of SAE latents reveals interpretable structure aligned with route intent, vehicle speed, and braking behavior, recovering route intent with 98.3% accuracy without supervision. Through paired counterfactual image edits, we further show that specific SAE features are visually grounded and systematically respond to scene changes such as traffic light state and stop sign presence. Steering individual SAE latents produces predictable, monotonic changes in planner outputs including lateral displacement, curvature, and braking. Finally, we demonstrate a practical application of these representations: we build a lightweight adapter trained on SAE latents that reduces trajectory selection error by 3.44%, outperforming an equivalent adapter that omits SAE latents, confirming that the sparse representation captures useful information for interpretability. Code and visualizations are available at https://mgagvani.github.io/ mechanistic-interpretability-for-e2e-driving/.

nBwRDRUdMc.a: Real-world environments are messy, with paths often blocked by everyday objects like chairs and toys, requiring robots to perform interactive navigation by manipulating obstacles to clear a path. Existing methods rely on extensive simulation-based learning or per-scene instructions specifying which objects to avoid or manipulate. They struggle to generalize across novel objects, diverse environments, and varied contexts such as a cart of fragile glassware that should be avoided while an empty one can be pushed. We formalize this problem as open-world interactive navigation and present MessyNav, a zero-shot framework based on vision-language models (VLMs). At its core, MessyNav performs explicit VLM-based affordance reasoning before task planning to decide whether to swipe, pick up, or avoid an object and produce a high-level plan. Evaluated on a mobile manipulator across real-world indoor and outdoor environments, MessyNav improves success rate by 27 percentage points (pp) over the strongest baseline in real-robot trials and achieves statistically significant gains in a larger-scale offline evaluation, without task-specific training.
nBwRDRUdMc.k: Mobile Manipulation, Interactive Navigation, Affordance Reasoning

0rvhGgRYjx.a: Robots deployed in delivery, campus, and emergency-response settings often need to navigate from buildings to streets within a single continuous episode. Existing benchmarks usually evaluate indoor and outdoor navigation separately, and many abstract away robot execution, leaving exit finding, boundary traversal, adaptation, and kinodynamic failures underexplored. We introduce NAV V ERSE, a physics-enabled benchmark for indoor-to-street embodied navigation. NAV V ERSE contains 100 indoor scenes, 50 urban outdoor scenes, and 50 indoor-to-street scenes, and 10,000 episodes spanning Object Navigation, Vision-and-Language Navigation, and Place Navigation tasks, where agents search for semantic points of interest such as restaurants or banks. Agents are evaluated through executable robot interfaces using task-success, path-efficiency, and safety metrics. Zero-shot experiments with RL, VLA, and modular baselines show that current agents remain far from solving cross-context navigation: end-to-end VLAs obtain the highest zero-shot success, while the modular method provides the strongest safety profile. PlaceNav further reveals a clear drop from outdoor to indoor-to-street scenes, indicating that adaptation remains a major bottleneck. Training with supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning improves performance on both object and place goals, while Go2-W experiments demonstrate transfer of NavVerse finetuning to real-world navigation. Project website: https://umich-curly.github.io/NavVerse-Benchmark/.

F4IB3mxHbO.a: Recent perception-free end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving methods bypass explicit perception outputs by compressing dense image patch tokens into compact scene tokens for downstream trajectory generation and scoring. While these scene tokens form a compact visual bottleneck for the planner, they receive supervision solely from the planning objective, providing limited constraints on the encoded visual information. To address this limitation, we introduce Neural Token Reconstruction (NTR), a representation learning framework to directly constrain the compact scene-token bottleneck in perception-free driving. NTR introduces a self-distillation masked latent reconstruction objective that reconstructs masked patch-level latent features using only compact scene tokens as reconstruction memory. This forces reconstruction gradients to pass exclusively through the scene-token bottleneck, encouraging scene tokens to preserve richer and less redundant visual representations for planning. We further introduce semantic priors derived from foundation-model annotations as a weak semantic interface biasing reconstruction targets toward driving-related structures without introducing explicit perception heads. All auxiliary reconstruction components are removed at inference time, leaving the deployed planner unchanged. NTR achieves state-of-the-art performance on three public autonomous driving benchmarks, including 8.0461 RFS on Waymo E2E and 94.1 PDMS / 90.9 EPDMS on NavSim1&2. The learned scene tokens exhibit lower pairwise redundancy and higher effective rank, indicating that effective bottleneck supervision improves both compact visual representation learning and planning performance. We further validate NTR on a private large-scale driving dataset and integrate it into a real-vehicle planning stack, demonstrating its practical applicability beyond public benchmarks. Real-world deployment videos are available at https://youtu.be/xVRq1oDzBrw?si=WRPDBOJsYRoR74FE.
F4IB3mxHbO.k: End-to-End Autonomous Driving, Masked Latent Reconstruction, Scene Representation Learning

oJTM5ysEeJ.a: Olfaction provides critical information about airborne chemical cues, yet it remains largely underexplored in embodied AI, with limited prior machine olfaction work focusing primarily on semantic odor perception. We introduce OdorSpaces, a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visualolfactory embodied navigation. OdorSpaces augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion simulated by Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), enabling agents to navigate photorealistic indoor environments using both visual and olfactory observations. The benchmark includes two representative source-seeking scenarios: invisible gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization. We develop an initial multimodal reinforcement learning policy that integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time. Experiments show that the policy outperforms a diverse set of baselines, establishing a strong reference for future research on visual-olfactory embodied navigation.
oJTM5ysEeJ.k: Visual-Olfactory Learning, Machine Olfaction, Embodied Navigation

bXQv3Kn5qL.a: A navigation agent must understand high-level semantic instructions and reason about precise spatial structure. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), with their strong generalization, are a promising foundation for such agents. We propose GTA, a decoupled design that separates low-level spatial state estimation from high-level semantic planning. We introduce an explicit metric world representation that combines accumulated geometry with navigation history and exposes this information to the MLLM through a multimodal interface for decision-making. We further introduce counterfactual branch reasoning that checks anticipated outcomes against subsequent observations and revises navigation decisions when they disagree. The world representation grounds waypoint selection in reconstructed metric geometry. GTA achieves 48.8% Success Rate (SR) on the full R2R-CE val-unseen split and 46.2% on a 260-episode English RxR-CE val-unseen subset. Additional comparisons on shared R2R-CE episodes and mechanism ablations support the framework’s effectiveness. We also demonstrate transfer to wheeled, quadrupedal, and aerial robots. Project page: https://zeruili22.github.io/GTA/

7BCkvvmpuj.a: Monocular depth estimation has achieved strong open-domain generalization, yet reliable robotic deployment remains difficult in transparent, reflective, and specular environments, where depth sensors often produce missing or biased depth. Existing methods often handle such optical failures with scenespecific preprocessing, auxiliary modules, or post-hoc fine-tuning. While effective in constrained settings, these designs increase architectural redundancy and can over-specialize general geometry models to narrow optical scenarios. We revisit this problem as a localized failure mode within base-model training and identify sensor-induced supervision bias as a key bottleneck: models inherit sensor failure patterns from biased real-depth supervision in optically challenging regions. We then introduce OptiGeo, a bias-aware training framework that rehabilitates biased real supervision using a clean-geometry teacher and residual-trimmed alignment. We redefine transparency-targeted rendering as a compact source of clean optical geometry, rather than a large domain-specific fine-tuning set. With only a small targeted rendering set, OptiGeo learns the geometric structure of transparent objects and regions, correcting local geometry distortions that real sensors cannot reliably supervise. Despite only 30M parameters, OptiGeo outperforms substantially larger 300M-scale monocular models and billion-scale multi-view baselines on transparent-scene benchmarks, while remaining competitive on general zeroshot depth and boundary sharpness. Real-world navigation cases further validate its practicality as an efficient perception module in optically challenging scenes. Project page: https://mx-liu6.github.io/OptiGeo-web/
7BCkvvmpuj.k: Monocular Geometry, Optical Robustness, Embodied Perception

hr2FYFod4n.a: A mobile robot following a graph of known routes can make costly navigation errors when a temporary obstacle blocks a critical edge: waiting too long behind a parked cart wastes time, but immediately rerouting around a person who would move in a few seconds is also inefficient. Standard reactive obstacle avoidance addresses local motion around obstacles, while fixed wait-or-reroute rules ignore how long different obstacle types tend to persist. We propose OSCAR: an adaptive survival-modeling framework for graph-based navigation with temporary blockages. Assuming obstacle class labels are available at encounter time, the robot learns class-conditioned residual clearance-time distributions from online experience, including right-censored observations when it reroutes before observing clearance. These survival models are integrated into a time-dependent graph planner that maintains obstacle memory and computes a patience threshold at each blocked edge: how long to wait before taking an alternate route. The method continuously updates its clearance estimates across episodes and uses them to balance waiting against rerouting. We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real mobile robot in a university atrium with obstacles including people, chairs, bins, and tubes. In simulation, the learned policy’s time-to-goal converges to within 1% of an oracle with access to ground-truth clearance distributions after fewer than 20 observations per obstacle class, outperforming all heuristic baselines. Realworld deployment confirms that the policy improves online, adapting its patience thresholds from experience across 50 navigation episodes.
hr2FYFod4n.k: Robot Navigation; Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance; Survival Analysis; Adaptive Planning; Online Learning

rwx9GCSVjH.a: Generalist visual-navigation policies tell a robot which direction to go but not how far. A separate lifting step is needed at deployment to convert their unitless trajectory into a metric path that a controller can track; existing scalar lifters apply uniform scaling that misses per-waypoint corrections, while in-policy approaches that inject monocular depth into the policy inherit the prediction errors of the depth model near obstacles and at close range. We present PathLift, a per-waypoint depth-conditioned adapter that lifts a pre-trained visual-navigation policy by consuming an explicit, sensor-grade depth source (RGB-D, stereo, or projected LiDAR) and fitting per-waypoint magnitude and lateral residuals to a canonicalized prior. PathLift consistently improves closed-loop navigation across diverse visual-navigation policies in simulation and on a real wheeled robot under both stereo and LiDAR depth. By turning the policy’s unitless intent into a depth-feasible metric path in a single feed-forward pass, the adapter lifts realworld success without test-time optimization.

Sal8Urvt1F.a: Bird’s-eye-view (BEV) images have been demonstrated to provide valuable prior information for navigation. Given the global information provided by such views, two key challenges remain: how to fully exploit this information and how to reliably use it during execution. In this paper, we propose a navigation system that uses BEV images as global priors and is designed for ground and near-ground robotic platforms. The system employs an image generation model to interpret human intent from natural language, identify the target destination, and generate traversability masks. During execution, we introduce cross-view localization to align the robot’s odometry with the BEV map and mitigate long-term drift in conventional odometry. We conduct extensive benchmark experiments to evaluate the proposed method and further validate its effectiveness on both UAV and quadruped robot platforms. Using only a conventional local motion planner, the quadruped robot successfully completes a 285-meter outdoor long-range navigation task. This work demonstrates how the world-understanding capabilities of foundation models can be transferred to embodied navigation, enabling robots to benefit from the strong generalization ability of existing image generation models.
Sal8Urvt1F.k: Robot Navigation, BEV Prior, Foundation Models, Cross-view Localization, Image Generation Model

DyO8vc0zYK.a: Safe formation navigation requires a robot team to reach task goals while avoiding collisions and maintaining a desired formation geometry. In this multi-robot cooperative task, navigation progress, collision avoidance, and formation maintenance often impose competing requirements on the team. Existing approaches commonly combine these requirements through weighted scalar objectives or treat safety as an isolated constraint, making it difficult to explicitly represent and resolve their asymmetric priorities. We formulate safe formation navigation as a prioritized multi-constraint coordination problem with an explicit hierarchy: safety constraints take the highest priority, formation maintenance is enforced whenever safety permits, and navigation progress is optimized under these higher-priority requirements. To realize this hierarchy, we develop a learningbased coordination framework that supports decentralized execution and uses online estimates of safety risk and formation degradation to regulate each robot’s behavior while preserving the specified priority order. This enables the team to prioritize collision avoidance, temporarily relax the formation when necessary, recover the desired structure after local conflicts, and continue goal-directed navigation. We evaluate the method in VMAS-based formation-navigation scenarios with static and dynamic obstacles, and further demonstrate the learned policy on a fleet of omnidirectional AGVs.
DyO8vc0zYK.k: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning, Multi-Robot Formation Navigation, Prioritized Constraints

EsZGt1eIZr.a: End-to-end autonomous driving models are typically trained on offline human-demonstration datasets that provide limited state coverage and often no closed-loop feedback, making them prone to compounding errors when deployed in closed-loop and brittle to long-tail agent interactions. To overcome these limitations, we propose an alternative strategy for training end-to-end driving models: large-scale self-play directly from pixels in simulation. While prior self-play approaches have shown promising transfer to human-driven traffic in simulation, they typically assume vectorized Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) observations that are incompatible with end-to-end policies operating directly on sensor observations. To this end, we introduce Gigapixel, a high-throughput batched driving simulator with perspective rendering, enabling scalable self-play directly from pixel observations. Rather than targeting compute-costly photorealistic sensor simulation, Gigapixel renders a simplified bounding-box world that preserves essential scene structure while achieving throughput at 50k agent steps per second. Since direct pixel-space self-play RL is prohibitively sample-inefficient at end-to-end model scale, we propose self-play DAgger training: we train pixel-based policies in selfplay via on-policy distillation from a privileged RL teacher. To bridge the sim-toreal gap, we subsequently transfer the self-play trained policies to real-world sensor data through lightweight perception adaptation. Policies trained in Gigapixel and adapted to real sensor data achieve competitive performance on the HUGSIM and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks without human trajectory supervision. Moreover, scaling self-play training yields consistent gains in policy performance, establishing self-play as a practical and scalable strategy for training end-to-end models.

foRrdaQ3mz.a: Zero-shot object navigation (ZSON) requires robots to find target objects in unseen environments without task-specific fine-tuning or pre-built maps, a key capability for general-purpose service robots. Yet methods that perform well in simulation often degrade in cluttered real-world scenes with severe occlusion and latent hazards, where large unseen regions make single-scene inference brittle and unsafe. We propose Schrödinger’s Navigator, a belief-aware framework that reasons at inference time over multiple trajectory-conditioned imagined 3D futures. Given candidate paths, a trajectory-conditioned 3D world model predicts hypothetical observations and maintains a superposition of plausible scene realizations rather than committing to one map. An adaptive occluder-aware sampler directs imagination to uncertainty-critical regions, while a Future-Aware Value Map (FAVM) aggregates imagined futures for robust, proactive action selection. Experiments in simulation and on a physical Go2 quadruped show that Schrödinger’s Navigator outperforms strong ZSON baselines, improving hidden-target discovery and risk-aware waypoint selection in occlusion-heavy navigation scenarios. These results highlight imagined 3D futures as a promising foundation for a modular, scalable, and generalizable framework for zero-shot navigation in uncertain real-world environments.
foRrdaQ3mz.k: Zero-Shot Object Navigation, Generative Scene Imagination

8xaYRUduNe.a: Control-space tree search sidesteps the steering requirement of geometric search methods and offers an asymptotic route to natively feasible kinodynamic trajectories. In practice, however, control-space search fails on the simplest of motion-planning instances for nonlinear systems such as quadrotors. This failure is rooted in poor geometric coverage induced when naive control-sampling measures are pushed forward through system dynamics. We resolve this problem by learning a lightweight sampler whose pushforward achieves low geometric dispersion in the local search space. The central idea is to utilize a well-dispersed reference map as a training scaffold, eliminating the need for an external expert. Our experiments then demonstrate that the learned sampler enables control-space search for quadrotor motion planning when naive sampling measures simply fail. Once enabled, controlspace planning using a batched forward-propagation tree is shown to outperform state-of-the-art planners in obstacle-rich environments. We also show that the geometric reach of the learned model dominates popular motion primitive libraries, spanning roughly thrice their volume. Arbitrarily low-dispersion primitives are thus made available for any state merely by scaling test-time compute. 0.4 0.2 0.3 0.1 0.2 0.0 0.1 -0.1 z (m) y (m)
8xaYRUduNe.k: Kinodynamic motion planning, Learning for planning, Quadrotor flight

wBzyyPlFs6.a: Urban sidewalk navigation presents significant challenges due to complex structural layouts, dynamic pedestrian behaviors, and long distances. While recent visual navigation models offer a promising solution, the lack of a unified benchmark hinders quantitative and reproducible evaluation. To bridge this gap, we propose SidewalkBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed for visual navigation on urban sidewalks. Built upon NVIDIA Isaac Sim, SidewalkBench brings GPU-accelerated simulation of diverse, high-fidelity sidewalk environments, including both procedurally generated and real-world scanned scenes. We further populate the scenes with rich, reactive event-based pedestrian behaviors and flexible, efficient animation, enabling standardized model evaluation under realistic real-world settings. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 9 visual navigation models on 330 unit-test scenarios, 800 pedestrian-reactive scenarios, and 105 long-horizon scenarios. Our findings highlight that pedestrian interaction and long-horizon robustness remain critical bottlenecks for existing models, and scaling up sidewalk training with synthetic data emerges as a promising solution.
wBzyyPlFs6.k: Visual Navigation Benchmark, Urban Sidewalk Simulation

nYkpEYmvbg.a: Recent embodied navigation methods leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong generalization. However, reliable path planning in complex environments remains challenging due to insufficient spatial awareness. The key challenge lies in learning spatial awareness that generalizes across diverse scenes and supports cross-task navigation reasoning. Motivated by this challenge, we propose SPAN-Nav, which advances generalized 3D spatial awareness for embodied navigation by estimating egocentric 3D occupancy from RGB video streams and using it as an intermediate spatial representation for navigation reasoning. SPAN-Nav represents 3D occupancy in a continuous latent space and projects it into a compact spatial token for VLM integration. This design provides navigation-relevant geometric cues while avoiding the inference overhead of dense volumetric representations. To align occupancy perception with navigation reasoning, SPAN-Nav adopts Two-Stage Spatial-to-Action Alignment (S2A-Align), a training strategy that first grounds navigation decisions on groundtruth occupancy and then adapts action reasoning to self-predicted spatial priors to reduce the training-inference gap. Based on a large-scale dataset with 4.2M occupancy annotations across diverse scenes and navigation tasks, SPAN-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance on Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN), urban navigation and point-goal navigation benchmarks, improving Success Rate (SR) by 4.6%/ 5.3% on R2R-CE / RxR-CE, reducing MetaUrban collision cost by over 4×, and reaching 90.9% / 91.0% zero-shot SR on InternVLA-N1 System-1 pointgoal navigation benchmark. Real-world experiments further demonstrate robust obstacle avoidance and reliable execution in cluttered environments.
nYkpEYmvbg.k: Embodied Navigation, Spatial Awareness, Occupancy Prediction

ODfnFGIIe3.a: Reliable trajectory planning under partial observability depends not only on computing a feasible geometric path, but also on whether the robot receives informative observations while executing that trajectory. Existing approaches usually keep the environment fixed and adapt the robot through beliefspace planning, active localization, or added sensing, often incurring costly uncertainty propagation and brittle behavior in observation-poor regions. We flip this perspective and address the largely open problem of task-aware environment augmentation: given a mapped environment, a planned task trajectory, and a small budget of visual fiducial markers, where should the environment be augmented so that the planned trajectory can be executed reliably under uncertainty?
