On a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, across three pick-and-place tasks of increasing whole-body difficulty and three VLA backbones (ψ0 , π0.5 , GR00T N1.6), a policy trained purely on LEGS data matches or exceeds one trained on human teleoperation demos on every experiment. It also outperforms a mesh-only baseline trained on the same motions without the calibrated 3DGS frontend. Because motion is recorded independently of appearance, the same demonstrations can be re-rendered for a target scene and objects at over 15× lower cost than teleoperation. When both the objects and the scene change, a policy trained on LEGS- AUG data re-rendered for that target maintains task success, while the teleop baseline fails entirely. Code and videos are available at https://hojjunekim.github.io/legs/.
0jY75QYDMn.k: Humanoid, Sim-to-real Transfer, Robot Data Generation, Robot Simulator, Loco-Manipulation, Vision Language Action Model

802PZFmFGd.a: Physical control tasks in the natural world, such as driving or object manipulation, frequently exhibit dramatic variations in sensory and compute complexity over time. Correspondingly, a natural resource-efficient choice for robot control is to dynamically switch between control modes with varying resource allocations. However, such “mode-switching controllers” (MSCs) have historically required laborious, expert-driven design and synthesis for each new task. Driven by these design difficulties, modern robotic control architectures often fall back to a wasteful “monolithic” one-size-fits-all structure, where resource allocation is permanently anchored to the hardest, most resource-intensive task phases. To facilitate the design of performant yet efficient MSCs, we propose LLM-Guided synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures (LEMCA). LEMCA represents MSC designs as interpretable programs to be iteratively refined in an evolutionary loop. To evaluate design fitness, we propose MSC-compatible extensions of automated controller synthesis approaches, such as reinforcement learning in simulation. LEMCA then leverages the semantic priors, reasoning, and coding capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively edit controller modes, their corresponding sensory-compute resource allocations, and mode transitions. Our experiments across diverse control benchmarks show that LEMCA consistently discovers strategies that surpass the Pareto frontier of monolithic designs by reclaiming wasted resources during “easy” task phases. LEMCA thus presents an automated, low-effort path to synthesize resource-efficient MSC designs. Project Website: https://lemca-robotics.github.io/

7qMRpmvhZL.a: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation; however, their transition to real-world environments reveals vulnerabilities to minor environmental perturbations. We propose FLARE, an optimization framework that exploits these vulnerabilities via targeted illuminations, causing critical disruption of baseline tasks. While adversarial training is the standard countermeasure, we identify a critical and previously underestimated defensive pitfall: naive data augmentations condition VLA models to largely discard color as noise, biasing their visual perception toward shape cues. We expose this degradation through a diagnostic grayscale evaluation, in which a naively defended model maintains high success rates on grayscale inputs, while its success rate on benign, color-dependent real-world tasks drops to at most 48.8%, compared with 78.8% for the undefended SmolVLA baseline. To address this, we propose ChromaGuard, a chroma-preserving adversarial training method. On a physical 6-DoF robotic platform using SmolVLA, we demonstrate that ChromaGuard achieves 95.0% and 88.8% success rates in benign and attacked color-dependent tasks, respectively. Demo videos are available at https://keio-csg.github.io/ChromaGuard/.
7qMRpmvhZL.k: Policy evaluation, adversarial scenarios generation, and red teaming, Vision-Language-Action Models, Adversarial Robustness

eRpTR7EEC1.a: Autonomous robots often need to move their camera before they can act: to inspect an object, reveal an occluded region, or obtain a view that responds to a user’s intent. While vision-language navigation translates instructions to base motion and vision-language-action policies map instructions to manipulation actions, vision-language conditioned camera motion remains comparatively underexplored as a first-class action. We formulate vision-language conditioned camera motion generation: given a current RGB observation and a free-form naturallanguage intent, predict a relative target camera pose for the next observation. The challenge is that useful viewpoint changes depend on latent perceptual intent, ranging from coarse spatial moves to fine-grained inspection or occlusion revealing. To model this structure, we mine multi-intent camera-motion supervision from egocentric video via hindsight labeling, pairing each relative SE(3) target pose with plausible intents and observation-gain descriptions inferred from the reached view. We propose LIME, a vision-language camera-motion generator that combines an autoregressive observation-gain output with a continuous flowmatching pose head. This design lets the model jointly predict what the next view should reveal while representing multi-hypothesis target views. Across viewpointprediction experiments and downstream robotic tasks, we show that LIME learns intent-conditioned camera motion from passive egocentric video, turning ordinary human recordings into supervision for a reusable active-perception primitive that supports general-purpose viewpoint selection, manipulation, embodied question answering, and mid-distance navigation.
eRpTR7EEC1.k: Active Perception, Vision-Language Conditioned Camera Motion, Egocentric Video

SBGylS4zwM.a: Realizing true end-to-end biological laboratory automation requires robotic systems that can support two essential capabilities: directly manipulating liquids, and preparing and clearing the programmable automated liquid-handler platforms through which liquids are ultimately processed. However, existing laboratory benchmarks such as AutoBio and LabUtopia focus on rigid-body instrument operations or chemistry procedures with liquid checks based on tool or object states. We introduce LiquidLab, a robotic benchmark to jointly evaluate physically grounded liquid manipulation and automated liquid-handler operation for biological laboratory automation, comprising sixteen tasks across direct liquid manipulation, platform operations, and long-horizon wet-lab protocols. We further propose a parallel SPH fluid simulation pipeline built on Genesis that enables large-scale parallel liquid simulation on a single GPU, and ground task success in particle-based pouring and filling criteria alongside task-specific checks. Benchmarking six representative imitation-learning and vision-language-action policies reveals that current models remain far from reliable. Failures are concentrated in millimeter-scale labware staging and free-surface fluid control, exposing a clear gap between current robotic capabilities and the demands of fully autonomous biology. Project website: https://liquidlab-bench.github.io/.
SBGylS4zwM.k: Vision-Language-Action Models, Laboratory Automation, Liquid Manipulation, Automated Liquid Handling, Imitation Learning

n31eEof0k3.a: Long-horizon manipulation remains challenging for vision-languageaction (VLA) policies: real tasks are multi-step, progress-dependent, and brittle to compounding execution errors. We present LoHo-Manip, a modular framework that scales short-horizon VLA execution to long-horizon instruction following via a dedicated task-management VLM. The manager is decoupled from the executor and is invoked in a receding-horizon manner: given the current observation, it predicts a progress-aware remaining plan that combines (i) a subtask sequence with an explicit done + remaining split as lightweight language memory, and (ii) a visual trace—a compact 2D keypoint trajectory prompt specifying where to go and what to approach next. The executor VLA is adapted to condition on the rendered trace, thereby turning long-horizon decision-making into repeated local control by “following the trace.” Crucially, predicting the remaining plan at each step yields an implicit closed loop: failed steps persist in subsequent outputs, and traces update accordingly, enabling continuation and replanning without hand-crafted recovery logic or brittle visual-history buffers. Extensive experiments spanning embodied planning, long-horizon reasoning, trajectory prediction, and end-to-end manipulation in simulation and on a real Franka robot demonstrate strong gains in long-horizon success, robustness, and out-of-distribution generalization.
n31eEof0k3.k: Long-horizon Manipulation, Vision Language Action Models, Vision Language Models

4M7C3PsA78.a: Open-world mobile manipulation requires a robot to find an object, approach it, and move it to a target receptacle from a language instruction. Training vision-language model (VLM) agents for these tasks requires demonstrations of both action selection and active vision. Existing pipelines often convert planned trajectories into high-level action labels, but shortest-path progress provides limited supervision for deciding where to look. We introduce Agent-Interface Data Alignment (AIDA), a data collection pipeline in which a teacher directly selects and executes actions through the deployed agent’s skill interface. For mobile manipulation, we design teachers that maintain target visibility, recover lost targets, and approach for picking or placing. We add template-based spatial reasoning supervision and use a shared harness to organize observations, history, and outputs during training and inference. The resulting agent, AIDA-OWMM, achieves 71.76% full-task success on 170 held-out OWMM episodes. Teacher sensitivity analysis shows that active-vision demonstrations improve student success. The simulation-trained agent achieves 38% end-to-end success on a real mobile robot without additional training. Applying AIDA to a navigation subset of EmbodiedBench further demonstrates the pipeline’s utility for navigation tasks. Project website.
4M7C3PsA78.k: Open-world mobile manipulation, vision-language model agents, imitation learning

2AOAVWqGC6.a: Multi-camera perception is a load-bearing pillar of indoor robot manipulation, yet current feed-forward 3D foundation models still provide only centimeter-level camera poses on cluttered manipulation rigs. In our RH20T setting, off-the-shelf COLMAP and RGB-D ICP can degrade rather than reliably improve WorldMirror-v2 initializations. We present latent score-based pose refinement (LSPR), a foundation-init-conditioned calibration method that repurposes diffusion from global pose generation into local residual refinement on the SE(3) tangent space. LSPR learns the score field of the residual poseerror distribution induced by a strong initializer: ground-truth rigs are corrupted by tangent-space perturbations covering the initializer’s small-noise regime, and inference follows this field from the foundation initialization rather than sampling poses from noise. To make this local refinement reliable, LSPR combines score-level ensembling, hard-tier sample mining, and a confidence gate that falls back to the initializer under distribution shift. On held-out RH20T manipulation scenes, LSPR improves WorldMirror-v2 initializations from centimeterlevel to sub-centimeter, sub-degree Sim(3)-aligned accuracy, and these calibration gains transfer to downstream multi-view depth fusion. Our code is available at: https://github.com/NebulaMWF/lspr.
2AOAVWqGC6.k: Multi-camera calibration, Score-based diffusion, Pose refinement

GFxjqZVSND.a: Multi-Modal Motion Planning (M3 P) requires joint reasoning over continuous motions and discrete mode transitions, making it difficult to solve efficiently. For instance, a bipedal robot may walk to a target location and then use its arms to grasp an object. This scenario captures both mode transitions and continuous dynamics, yielding feasible paths that neither purely discrete nor continuous planners can handle. While Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) offers a principled framework, constructing tractable formulations for non-convex problems is typically manual and domain-specific, especially in the approximate, discretization-based MIP regime needed for non-convex robotic tasks. We propose M3 P-R1, a reinforcement learning method that fine-tunes large language models (LLMs) to decompose M3 P tasks into MIP variables, constraints, and objectives. Instead of directly outputting answers—often prone to hallucination—the model generates executable Python code using MIP optimization libraries and constraint interfaces. This enables solver-backed execution for robust and verifiable solutions. Trained with an outcome-driven reward against the solver, M3 P-R1 learns to compose modality-level discretization primitives and synthesize cross-modal coupling constraints, producing executable MIP programs for complex M3 P tasks. We further introduce LLMM3 P Bench, a benchmark of 1,316 problems spanning 5 single-modal and 8 multi-modal compositions, and use it to evaluate the proposed method. Experiments show that M3 PR1 achieves 91.7% single-modal and 80.9% multi-modal task success rate, improving over the strongest prompt-only LLM baseline (GPT-5.2) by 26.4 and 40.6 percentage points, respectively. M3 P-R1 further transfers to real-world hardware at 87.5% success rate. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of solver-grounded LLM reasoning for reliable motion planning. Project page: https://github.com/XingpengSun0/CoRL-26-M3P-R1
GFxjqZVSND.k: Multi-Modal Motion Planning, LLM for Robot Planning

BxW31Dilgn.a: Today’s dominant route to generalist robots scales robotics data to train end-toend policies. We instead use a vision-language model (VLM) as a coding agent that writes robot programs using a curated library of perception, planning, and control tools. MAESTRO’s orchestration harness packages multi-step perception and action procedures into callable tools and guides their use through a plan–act– replan loop, using visual and execution feedback to verify outcomes and recover from failures. With this tool library and harness, MAESTRO matches or surpasses state-of-the-art vision-language-action (VLA) models zero-shot in our tabletop comparison and performs diverse mobile manipulation tasks, without collecting new teleoperation data or invoking a VLA tool. Ablations show that expanding the tool library improves average task progress with the full harness, while adding tools without it does not reliably improve progress. Additional case studies examine cross-trial code improvement, VLA tool use, and autonomous seed demonstrations for downstream data augmentation. We argue that such agentic systems offer a complementary, far less-explored axis to data scaling for general-purpose robots. Project site: maestro-robot.github.io. Code: github.com/Beethoven-Q/maestro.
BxW31Dilgn.k: VLM agents, robotic manipulation, zero-shot generalization

zr63f3tmyq.a: Generalist robot manipulation requires a single vision-language-action (VLA) policy to execute diverse skills across scenes and instructions. However, current multi-skill VLA policies often leave two aspects of an instruction insufficiently modeled: which primitive skill to execute and where/how to contact and move objects. We propose MAST-VLA (Multi-skill Adaptation with Skillconditioned experts and Trajectory-affordance priors), a dual-conditioning framework for robot manipulation. MAST-VLA introduces skill-conditioned LoRA Mixture-of-Experts (LoRA-MoE) adapters in the LLM backbone, where skillquery tokens and routing biases guide low-rank expert specialization, and converts a predicted affordance heatmap into a patch-level trajectory-affordance spatial prior for the action head. On the CALVIN ABC→D long-horizon multi-skill cross-scene generalization setting, MAST-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching an Avg. Len of 4.65 over five-subtask evaluation sequences. Real-robot multi-skill sequence experiments further validate its deployability under real perception and control noise.
zr63f3tmyq.k: Robot Manipulation, Vision-Language-Action Models, Multi-Task Learning, Affordance Learning

Br2rXixvyN.a: Despite growing interest in foundation models for robotic manipulation, systematic evaluation of their capabilities remains elusive. Existing benchmarks are either narrow and saturated, offering little signal on SOTA methods, broadly scoped, providing diversity at the cost of controlled experimentation, or require training on large, messy open-source datasets. We introduce MESA, an evaluation framework designed for precise, reproducible measurement of language-conditioned policy generalization. MESA provides five evaluation suites that isolate in-distribution performance and four distinct axes of generalization: spatial configuration, object instance, object category, and subtask composition, enabling researchers to diagnose where and why policies fail, not just whether they fail. To populate these suites at scale, we develop MESA-Gen, a pipeline for task and demonstration generation built by improving MimicGen. We instantiate the framework on two platforms and release both: the single-arm MESA suite, and BiMESA, the first large-scale benchmark for bimanual generalization. We evaluate seven baseline methods spanning diffusion policies, VLM-based approaches, and pretrained VLAs, finding that the strongest model achieves only 52% on MESA and 49% on BiMESA, providing meaningful signal while leaving ample room for progress. MESA rankings are broadly consistent with RoboArena scores, suggesting that MESA captures method-level differences relevant beyond simulation. Project website: https://pairlab.github.io/MESA.
Br2rXixvyN.k: Imitation Learning, Robot Foundation Models, Benchmarking

GqqwqejrTq.a: Mobile manipulators deployed across many rooms and visits should improve with experience. After discovering a cabinet is locked or finding an object in a drawer, a robot should reuse that knowledge rather than start each task from scratch. Yet today’s robots often treat each task as new: compact scene representations omit interaction-derived knowledge, video histories are difficult to query, and VLM planners reason without updating what the robot knows. We present MessyMem, a persistent memory system that enables mobile manipulators to learn from experience and reuse knowledge across tasks. MessyMem maintains a spatially grounded 3D scene graph of objects and locations, augments it with properties and outcomes learned through interaction, and links visual observations for fine-grained recall. We evaluate MessyMem in simulation and on a real mobile manipulator: in a continuous 25-task simulation lasting over 3 hours, MessyMem achieves 80.0% task progress, outperforming the strongest ablation by 14.8 percentage points and the strongest external baseline by 28.9 points, while retrieving task-relevant evidence from thousands of keyframes dating back over an hour.
GqqwqejrTq.k: Interaction-Grounded Memory, Mobile Manipulation, Scene Graph

qQs6JndxfZ.a: LLMs generate fluent plans for robots but routinely violate the syntactic and semantic constraints they must satisfy to execute, and existing remedies trade formal guarantees against plan quality: soft methods (affordance scoring, grounded decoding) give no guarantee, while symbolic planners (LLM+P) discard the LM’s commonsense. We propose Meta-Ctrl, a constrained-decoding framework that guarantees the encoded constraints while improving the base LM’s plan quality. Meta-Ctrl introduces meta-tokens, a compact vocabulary of grounded actions, and enforces syntax at the token level and semantics (preconditions, goals, ordering) at the action level. A meta-token HMM looks ahead over actions and weights each remaining valid plan by how likely the LM is to write it, steering decoding toward plans that are both valid and likely. The exact factorization keeps the semantic search at action granularity instead of compiling it into the token stream, which for a large VirtualHome task reduces the lookahead table from a theoretical ∼107 TB to ∼1.6 GB. With Meta-Ctrl, 8B and 20B open-weight models outperform every frontier model we evaluated on VirtualHome action sequencing in the Embodied Agent Interface, including Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5; on WAH-NL under the LoTa-Bench protocol, Llama 3.1 8B reaches the highest reported success rate. On a real tabletop robot, Meta-Ctrl reaches 100% plan validity. Project website: https://metactrlg.github.io
qQs6JndxfZ.k: Constrained Decoding, Formal Guarantees, Task and Motion Planning

wKRawikMuG.a: Humans understand and interact with the real world by relying on diverse physical feedback beyond visual perception. Motivated by this, recent approaches attempt to incorporate physical sensory signals into Vision-LanguageAction models (VLAs). However, they typically focus on a single type of physical signal, failing to capture the heterogeneous and complementary nature of real-world interactions. In this paper, we propose MoSS, a modular sensory stream framework that adapts VLAs to leverage multiple sensory signals for action prediction. Specifically, we introduce decoupled modality streams that integrate heterogeneous physical signals into the action stream via joint cross-modal self-attention. To enable stable incorporation of new modalities, we adopt a two-stage training scheme that freezes pretrained VLA parameters in the early stage. Furthermore, to better capture contact interaction dynamics, we incorporate an auxiliary task that predicts future physical signals. Through extensive real-world experiments, we demonstrate that MoSS successfully augments VLAs to leverage diverse physical signals (i.e., tactile, force, and torque), integrating multiple signals to achieve synergistic performance gains. The project page is available.

xOhVCWilYJ.a: Hierarchical VLM-based robotic systems often use sparse points or bounding boxes as intermediate spatial representations, which are inadequate for region-level grounding. This is particularly evident in instructions such as place near the bowl, which specify a feasible region rather than a single target point. We present RoboMAP, a VLM-based robotic grounding framework that uses adaptive affordance heatmaps as a language-conditioned intermediate interface between spatial reasoning and downstream modules. RoboMAP predicts dense score maps for continuous and object-free target regions, exposing feasible spatial support that downstream segmentation, grasping, and control modules can use beyond sparse prompts alone. To enable scalable training without manual dense labels, RoboMAP synthesizes heatmap supervision from heterogeneous annotations, including points, boxes, and robot trajectory data. Across four spatial grounding benchmarks evaluated with standard point-extraction metrics, RoboMAP obtains the best reported accuracy on three benchmarks while maintaining a 0.04 s grounding-stage forward pass. In 50 real-world dual-arm manipulation trials spanning five tabletop task types, it achieves an 82% success rate using heatmap-guided segmentation and grasp proposal. We further provide qualitative cross-embodiment demonstrations across manipulation and navigation scenarios. Project page: https://robo-map.github.io/.
xOhVCWilYJ.k: Spatial Grounding, Affordance Heatmaps, Vision-Language Models

k2QZxbcSbQ.a: Robust inertial odometry is essential for various carriers when external sensing is unreliable. Learning-based methods reduce integration drift by capturing local motion priors, but these methods often remain tied to a particular carrier, limiting generalization across heterogeneous platforms. We present MosaicIMU, a carrier-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) pretraining-andadaptation framework for generalizable neural inertial odometry. MosaicIMU uses a prototype-based router to compose carrier-specific expert features, decodes local velocity and uncertainty constraints, and integrates them with a historyaware EKF. For unseen domain adaptation, it freezes the pretrained base model and learns a new lightweight expert residual branch. For edge-deployment, it further reuses the router to select informative online samples for efficient incremental updates. Experiments show that MosaicIMU outperforms the strongest learningbased baseline, reducing average ATE and RTE-10s by 40% and 34%, respectively. These results highlight that MosaicIMU provides a scalable pretraining-todeployment paradigm for generalizable and adaptive neural inertial odometry.
k2QZxbcSbQ.k: Inertial Odometry, Mixture of Experts, Cross-Carrier Generalization, Online Adaptation Code: https://github.com/zoujy02/MosaicIMU

oKJnHTluoA.a: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly condition robot policies on history, depth, or 4D features to resolve ambiguity in long-horizon manipulation. However, more spatiotemporal evidence is not necessarily better: when the injected evidence is not motion-consistent, it can introduce geometric drift, fragmented temporal cues, and unstable action generation. This raises a simple question: should a VLA remember past frames, or remember the motion that connects them? We introduce MotionVLA, a motion-history interface that converts a short past-only video window into compact, time-continuous trajectory-field tokens. Instead of treating history as a sparse set of independently lifted frames, MotionVLA represents recent observations as physically coherent motion evidence. Current visual tokens query this history to retrieve task-relevant motion information, which is then recoupled into the VLA stream under trajectory-grounded supervision. Experiments across simulation benchmarks and real-robot rollouts show that MotionVLA improves long-horizon manipulation while producing more direct executions. These results suggest that effective VLA memory is not just about providing more 4D context, but about exposing motion-consistent evidence that is usable for control.
oKJnHTluoA.k: Vision-Language-Action Model, Motion History, Robot Learning

hPz010j4EA.a: Multi-hand semantic grasp generation aims to produce feasible, semantically appropriate grasp poses for different robotic hands from natural language instructions. Although the task is highly valuable, the lack of multi-hand grasp datasets with fine-grained contact descriptions between robotic hands and objects makes it a long-standing, difficult problem. In this paper, we present Multi-GraspSet, the first large-scale multi-hand grasp dataset with automatically annotated contacts. Based on Multi-GraspSet, we propose Multi-GraspLLM, a unified language-guided grasp generation framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to handle variable-length sequences and generate grasp poses for diverse robotic hands in a single unified architecture. Multi-GraspLLM first aligns the encoded point cloud features and text features into a unified semantic space. It then uses a flow-matching process to progressively transform a noise distribution into a target grasp pose conditioned on the fused semantics, with hand-specific decoders producing joint angles for each robotic hand. Experiments demonstrate improved grasp generation in simulation and the real world. For an unseen hand, LoRA with 10k samples (8.3% of 120k) achieves a success rate close to full-data training from scratch; 25k samples (20.8%) yield comparable or better performance across all metrics.
hPz010j4EA.k: Semantic grasp generation, Large language models, Grasp dataset

NEtxISu52Q.a: Robot manipulation often depends on sensory data beyond vision, especially in contact-rich tasks where force, tactile, or audio feedback reveals interaction states not directly visible from images. Yet such modalities are hardware- and taskspecific, and large multisensory datasets remain scarce, making it impractical to pretrain policies with every sensor they may encounter. We study multi-sensory continual learning: how to adapt a pretrained robot policy to new tasks with newly introduced modalities while preserving performance under the original sensor suite. We propose MultiSensory World Model (MuSe), which integrates limited multisensory data into pretrained vision-only. We find that multi-stage fusion, multisensory future prediction, and experience replay all drive better adaptation, and that policies pretrained with video prediction adapt better to new sensor modalities in finetuning. We instantiate MuSe by augmenting a pretrained vision-only World-Action Model with tactile force-torque sensing (enabling compliance control) and evaluate it on real-world manipulation tasks. Experiments show that MuSe not only performs well on contact-rich finetuning tasks but also has performance gains on pretraining tasks—suggesting that a modest multisensory dataset can enhance general model capability beyond the finetuning distribution.Project website: https://jadenvc.github.io/multisensory-continual-learning/
NEtxISu52Q.k: Imitation learning, World Models, Continual Learning

uhnmcdamCa.a: Vision-language-action (VLA) models rely on discrete action tokenizers to bridge continuous robot control and autoregressive sequence modeling, yet existing tokenizers often trade off between compression, latency, and downstream performance. We revisit this design through the lens of neural audio codecs—convolutional encoder–decoder architectures with residual vector quantization that serve as the standard front end for audio foundation models. Motivated by their success, we introduce the Neural Action Codec (NAC), which treats short robot action trajectories as multi-channel 1D signals and compresses them using a multi-scale RVQGAN architecture. We observe that audio-specific melspectrogram objectives are ill-suited for kinematic signals; however, by replacing them with simple time-domain and non-mel spectral reconstruction losses, audiocodec-style models can autoencode actions with high fidelity without substantial architectural changes. NAC provides a compact, ordered token space via offset codebooks, enabling standard autoregressive policies to operate over short, structured sequences. Meanwhile, a Vocos-style decoder with an ISTFT head and adversarial discriminators recovers smooth, detailed trajectories. Across LIBERO-10, RoboMimic, and a suite of real-world manipulation tasks, NAC achieves lower reconstruction error and higher success rates than binning, FAST, and prior VQbased tokenizers at comparable or better compression rates. These results demonstrate that repurposed neural audio codecs offer a strong, practical backbone for learned action tokenization in modern VLAs. 22
uhnmcdamCa.k: Action Tokenization, Manipulation, VLA, Behavioral Cloning

19iADsbO9A.a: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide strong language-conditioned manipulation knowledge, but they remain largely visiondriven and can struggle once manipulation enters contact states where the scene is occluded, depth is ambiguous, or small force errors push execution off the offline demonstration distribution. We present LIFT, Late Reactive Injection of Force for VLA Post-Training, a force-aware post-training framework that adds contact reactivity to a pretrained VLA policy while preserving its output at initialization. LIFT grafts a reactive action expert beside the original action expert, initializes it from pretrained action weights, and injects recent 6D end-effector force through causal force memory and zero-initialized cross attention, enabling actions to be refreshed during execution. To address the policy-dependent distribution shift of contact feedback, LIFT further couples reactive force injection with an online DAgger loop that trains on a mixture of offline task-alignment data and humancorrected online rollouts. Across towel folding, book insertion, and Hanoi ring placement, LIFT learns faster and reaches higher peak and final performance than vision-only DAgger, while ablations show that reactive force memory and online corrective data are both important for robust contact-rich manipulation. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/y-wng/lift.
19iADsbO9A.k: Force-Augmented Policies, Online Post-Training, Vision-LanguageAction Models

tAXtXe4Oqd.a: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across manipulation tasks, but remain brittle in precise physical interactions due to compounding execution errors. Can a reinforcement learning policy trained purely in simulation improve a real-world VLA zero-shot? We propose object-centric residual RL: a compact policy corrects a frozen VLA using object poses, proprioception, and the base action, avoiding image-based transfer and policy distillation. We replay the same teleoperation demonstrations in simulation to train a sim counterpart of the real VLA, providing a base for residual training without photorealistic reconstruction. The residual is trained only in simulation with pose noise and dropout, then deployed on the real robot without further adaptation. Across five manipulation tasks on a Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot, it improves average real-world success from 42% to 76%; successful corrected rollouts can also be reused for VLA self-improvement without additional teleoperation. Project page: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/ articles/object-centric-residual-rl/
tAXtXe4Oqd.k: Vision-Language-Action Models, Reinforcement Learning, Sim-toReal Transfer, Robot Manipulation

G6vrRbO3NE.a: Driver alerting based on dashcam videos requires sequential decisionmaking under partial observability: a system must warn early enough to support driver response, while avoiding frequent nuisance alerts. Existing approaches often reduce this problem to binary risk prediction, forcing a silent-or-alert decision even when visual evidence is uncertain. We propose VLA LERT, a vision–language alerting framework that casts warning generation as a tri-action policy over S ILENT, O BSERVE, and A LERT. The O BSERVE action serves as an internal evidencegathering state, allowing the system to defer uncertain warnings and adapt its subsequent observation window before committing an alert. VLA LERT uses a vision–language model (VLM) as a safety-evidence generator and pools hidden states from structured belief spans to form compact representations for danger estimation and policy prediction. We construct VLA LERT-Bench, a unified pertick benchmark from four real-world traffic accident video datasets, and introduce the Driver-Aware Utility Score (DAUS) to jointly evaluate ranking quality, event coverage, alert precision, and warning lead time. On the locked test split, sourcebalanced VLA LERT improves AUROC/AP from 0.519/0.158 to 0.679/0.254 over a representative collision-anticipation baseline under common validation-only calibration, and on VLA LERT-Bench validation it raises DAUS from 0.475 to 0.500. We further evaluate VLA LERT on 221 held-out ADAS takeover clips, where it improves R@5s from 74.2% to 88.7%. These results show improved risk discrimination and driver alerting utility, and suggest potential for early warning in takeover and roadside collision scenarios.
G6vrRbO3NE.k: Driver Alert System; Crash Prediction; VLM; Driving Safety

PEWWDUL10X.a: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown great promise as generalist policies for a large range of relatively simple tasks. However, they demonstrate limited performance on more complex tasks, such as those requiring complex spatial or semantic understanding, manipulation in clutter, or precise manipulation. We propose O MNI G UIDE, a flexible framework that improves VLA performance on such tasks by leveraging versatile sources of guidance, such as 3D foundation models, semantic-reasoning VLMs, and human pose models. We show how to naturally express many kinds of guidance as differentiable energy functions with task-specific attractors and repellers located in 3D space, that influence the sampling of VLA actions. In this way, O MNI G UIDE enables complementary taskrelevant guidance to improve a VLA model’s performance on challenging tasks. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, across diverse sources of guidance like collision safety and human demonstration, prove that O MNI G UIDE enhances the performance of state-of-the-art generalist policies (e.g., π0.5 , GR00T N1.6) significantly in terms of both success and safety rates. Critically, our unified framework matches or surpasses the performance of prior methods designed to incorporate specific sources of guidance into VLA policies. Project website: https://omniguide.github.io/
PEWWDUL10X.k: Vision-Language-Action Models, 3D Guidance Fields, Test-time Steering, Robot Manipulation “Put the Fruit in the purple bowl” Base Policy

fuB1LcFk9g.a: Robotic disassembly of end-of-life (EoL) products requires robots to accommodate product variation, follow prerequisite sequences, and approach components precisely for contact-rich manipulation. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides a practical path for adaptation, but limited and costly disassembly data cannot capture the distribution shifts arising from changing environments and product uncertainties. The policy’s own rollouts record its approach attempts, and human corrections demonstrate recovery from its errors, but turning these experiences into better policy performance remains challenging. We introduce PACER, a Process-Aware Correction and Evidence Reweighting framework that learns from these experiences through SFT, using progress toward the target and each trace’s source and outcome to weight valid action chunks in the native supervised action loss. PACER trains one policy per weighting setting and selects one of the resulting policies through held-out validation. We evaluate PACER on UR5e motherboard disassembly across five component classes, where it achieves 87/100 successful approach-and-handoff trials on the held-out benchmark, compared with 54/100 for vanilla post-SFT.

c5oiL7JqbQ.a: Humanoid behavior foundation models learn reusable whole-body policies from human motion priors, but typically assume that reference motions are compatible with the robot’s surroundings. When human and robot environments differ, the reference specifies behavior but not terrain-dependent footholds, clearance, support height, or contact timing. We introduce Perceptive Behavior Foundation Model (Perceptive BFM), a motion-conditioned policy pretrained on 16,813 clips (43.3 h) and reused without fine-tuning across unseen references, sources, and terrains. A robot-centric elevation grid supplies terrain information while the raw kinematic reference remains the command interface. Offline terrain-conformal reference synthesis (TCRS) adapts foot contacts and support height while preserving upper-body joint references. A blind teacher tracks these synthesized references and transfers its behavior through target-frame action alignment to a raw-reference student, an identity-gated Transformer tracker with zero-initialized terrain gates. In simulation, the deployed checkpoint completes 100% of flat-ground and 94.0% of 1,650 terrain trials across five behaviors and eleven slope, box, and stair cells, versus 19.5–23.4% for blind, no-TCRS, and no-map baselines. Map-corruption probes show that the policy conditions on terrain information. On hardware, the same checkpoint executes 35 motion classes over placed obstacles, including acrobatics and mocap teleoperation with operator–environment mismatch.
c5oiL7JqbQ.k: Humanoid control, Perceptive motion tracking, Behavior foundation models

A1Wg3RqdsR.a: Object navigation in unseen indoor environments requires agents to perform semantic search under partial observability. Vision-language models (VLMs) provide strong semantic-spatial priors for this task, but how to interface them with robot navigation remains challenging: dense VLM inference is expensive, while abstracting environments into symbolic memories often separates high-level reasoning from the raw visual evidence that supports it. We propose PIGEON (Point of Interest Guided Exploration for Object Navigation), a VLM-driven framework that formulates object navigation as a raw-observation-grounded sparse decision problem. PIGEON introduces Points of Interest (PoIs) as sparse visual decision units that couple geometrically executable waypoints with raw egocentric observations. Rather than using VLMs as dense controllers or restricting them to frontier ranking, PIGEON enables VLMs to select among task-critical PoIs, including exploration frontiers, suspected target objects, traversable stairs, and floor-level summaries, while low-level planners execute continuous motion between them. This PoI interface further makes high-level navigation decisions verifiable, allowing us to develop an RLVR pipeline that improves local VLMs without manual Chainof-Thought annotations. Extensive experiments on Habitat ObjectNav benchmarks show that PIGEON achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, scales consistently with foundation model capacity, and transfers to Active Embodied Question Answering with only prompt modifications. Real-world deployments on physical robots further demonstrate its robustness and efficiency.

2vx7I6aRPS.a: Post-training with real-world experience is critical for reliable deployment of robot foundation models, but heterogeneous data from demonstrations, human corrections, and autonomous rollouts are difficult to convert into stable policy updates. We present PIVOT, an iterative real-world post-training system built on Trust-Region Flow Matching Optimization (TRFO). TRFO provides a unified reinforcement-learning objective for heterogeneous deployment experience, using signed advantages to attract high-value transitions and repel low-value ones within a trust region while preserving the flow-matching training form. At each iteration, we first collect on-robot data using the current policy, estimate transition-level values via distributional TD learning, and then apply TRFO to update the policy. The updated policy is subsequently redeployed on the robot to gather the next round of experience, forming an iterative post-training procedure. On a suite of precise, contact-rich bimanual manipulation tasks, PIVOT yields consistent, monotonic gains over successive iterations, substantially improving success rates and throughput across all evaluated tasks. Project page: https://linshey.com/pivot/.

GMAZdF34n5.a: Learning to predict how the world evolves can provide vision-languageaction (VLA) policies with predictive context for long-horizon control, but its effectiveness depends on what future representation is modeled and how it conditions action generation. We introduce PLaW-VLA, which models task-relevant future states in a pretrained prediction-oriented representation space, reducing the need to predict control-irrelevant visual details. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, PLaW-VLA conditions action generation on observation history, current task semantics, and predicted future states through structured causal attention. Experiments show a +11.8 percentage-point (pp) gain over reactive policies on RoboTwin Hard Horizon III and a +1.77 pp gain over reconstruction-oriented latent prediction on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, supporting improved long-horizon control and generalization under distribution shift, respectively. By avoiding lowlevel visual reconstruction, PLaW-VLA lowers the burden of future prediction, enabling a lightweight latent world model with parallel future prediction and about 1/19 the inference latency of generative world–action modeling at comparable policy performance.

RRl1xXZLdM.a: Multi-fingered robots promise the speed and dexterity of human hands, yet challenging problems such as precise assembly have remained out of reach. These tasks are contact-rich, making data collection for imitation learning difficult, and sparse-reward, making direct exploration with reinforcement learning (RL) intractable. Consequently, prior work has made progress by structuring the problem with specialized grippers, tool attachments, and environment fixtures. In this work, we argue that before a robot can perfect precise assembly, it must first learn to play. We further ask the question: what factors in the process of learning to play matter for precise assembly? We propose Play2Perfect, an RL framework for task-agnostic pretraining through play on diverse objects and goals, which is then perfected on precise assembly. The goal of play is to acquire reusable manipulation priors, such as grasping, in-hand reorientation and pose reaching. Finetuning then adapts this general prior to assembly, focusing exploration on the final contact-rich, high-precision interactions needed for success. We systematically study key design choices in play pretraining, including object diversity, training objective, trajectory diversity, and goal precision. We show that our prior is 33x more sample-efficient than RL training from scratch, even when provided with dense, multi-stage rewards. We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, achieving 60% success on tight insertions with only 0.5 mm contact clearance, and over 50% success on long-horizon multi-part assembly and screwing.

JKoP9L6myQ.a: Robot actions vary in both extent and mode: how much change they produce and what kind of change they produce. A latent action space that reflects this structure may make it easier for downstream policies to map latent actions to robot actions. However, existing latent action methods typically rely on visual reconstruction from observation pairs without explicitly encouraging such structure. We introduce Polar Latent Actions with Radial structure (PoLAR), which imposes a radial-direction structure on latent actions, encouraging radius to encode transition extent and direction to retain transition mode. PoLAR uses temporal offsets between observations as a weak proxy for transition extent, encouraging transitions with larger offsets to occupy larger radii. We instantiate this structure in hyperbolic space, whose expanding volume with radius offers a natural fit for more diverse transition modes at larger extents. Across in-task and large-scale pretraining settings, PoLAR improves downstream policy performance in simulation and real-world robot experiments, outperforming latent action baselines and strong pretrained VLAs. These results suggest that structuring latent actions by extent and mode helps transfer visual pretraining to robot policy learning.

8YqfXYof0Y.a: Humans learn not only how their bodies move, but also how the surrounding world responds to their actions. In contrast, while recent VisionLanguage-Action (VLA) models exhibit impressive semantic understanding, they often fail to capture the spatiotemporal dynamics that govern physical interaction. In this paper, we introduce Pri4R, a simple yet effective approach that endows VLA models with an implicit understanding of world dynamics by leveraging privileged 4D information during training. Specifically, Pri4R augments VLAs with a lightweight point track head that predicts 3D point tracks. By leveraging VLA features within this head to jointly predict future 3D trajectories, the model learns to incorporate the evolving scene geometry into its shared representation space. This allows the action prediction components to leverage a more physically-aware context for precise control. Due to its architectural simplicity, Pri4R is seamlessly compatible with dominant VLA design patterns through minimal changes. During inference, we run the model using the original VLA architecture unchanged; Pri4R adds no extra inputs, outputs, or computational * Equal contribution. † Corresponding authors. overhead during inference. Across simulation and real world evaluations, Pri4R significantly improves performance on challenging manipulation tasks, including a +10% gain on LIBERO-Long and a +40% gain on RoboCasa. We further show that 3D point track prediction is an effective supervision target for learning action-world dynamics, while also validating our design choices through extensive ablations.

hvArz6F8eA.a: Safe human–robot collaboration requires more than visual description: a monitor must determine whether the robot body is safely separated, already colliding with the scene or a person, or about to collide. We call this capability collision grounding: binding visual observations to robot body geometry, camera viewpoint, scene layout, human proximity, and temporal motion in order to infer present and imminent contact. We introduce TouchSafeBench, a physics-grounded benchmark for evaluating collision grounding in vision-language models (VLMs). Built in Habitat 3.0, TouchSafeBench contains 2,940 simulated indoor co-presence episodes across social navigation and social rearrangement, with synchronized multi-view RGB-D, top-down maps, and simulator contact labels. We study two deploymentfacing tasks: classifying the current safety state and warning about imminent collision before contact. Across three frontier or robotics-oriented VLMs, nine visual representations, and three viewpoint configurations, current models remain far from reliable: the best Macro-F1 on either task is 56%, depth inputs are not automatically transformed into robot-body collision evidence, and robot–scene contact is consistently harder than human-contact risk. An expert human reaches 74% on the same clips, and the failure modes transfer to real recordings. TouchSafeBench reveals a central limitation of VLMs used as embodied safety monitors: visual fluency does not imply physical accountability. Reliable robot safety monitors will need representations that explicitly support collision grounding. The benchmark is available at https://jun25336-bit.github.io/TouchSafeBench/.
hvArz6F8eA.k: Human-Robot Collaboration, Robot Safety, Vision-Language Models, Collision Grounding

5oNzcK6SBR.a: Registering two captures of the same indoor space taken at different times underpins persistent spatial memory for robots and AR systems, yet the realistic version of this task is egocentric and its most scalable form is RGBonly. Head-mounted cameras yield blurry, fast-moving, partially overlapping views from which dense geometry is hard to recover. Classical registration leans on exactly the clean point clouds this setting lacks, while learned scene-graph methods require a pre-built or annotated graph and a trained matcher that we find brittle under egocentric data. We take a different route, using a pretrained vision-language model as the source of both scene understanding and cross-scan matching. Our method, PROSE (Prompted Scene rEgistration), lifts each RGB sequence into an object-level 3D scene graph using off-the-shelf foundation models for geometry, segmentation, and language, then prompts the same VLM to match object instances across the two RGB sequences. To make this matching tractable and reliable, we leverage object heights as a prior and verify each proposed match with a paired same/different query, then solve for the rigid transform by hypothesizing a candidate per matched object and selecting the one with the strongest geometric consensus. PROSE adds no learned parameters and requires no depth sensor, training, or annotated graph. On the egocentric Aria Digital Twin and Aria Everyday Activities benchmarks, it outperforms both geometric and learned scene-graph baselines in registration accuracy, on ground-truth and RGB-reconstructed point clouds alike, and the scene graph it produces transfers directly to downstream tasks.
5oNzcK6SBR.k: Scene Registration, Vision-Language Models, Egocentric Perception, Scene Graphs, Training-Free, 3D Scene Understanding

tfC6LMD02z.a: Generalist robot policies carry broad manipulation priors from largescale data, but specializing them to a new task remains the deployment bottleneck. This requires eliciting task-specific behavior from limited demonstrations without degrading their broad capabilities. We introduce Proxy Policy Steering (PPS), an inference-time adaptation method that resolves this challenge by training two lightweight proxy policies whose calibrated velocity-space difference steers the frozen base sampler. A reference proxy models the frozen base’s behavior on targettask observations, and a task proxy, initialized from the reference, captures how this behavior changes under task supervision. Their difference forms a calibrated velocity-space residual that steers the frozen base sampler at every denoising step. We identify the conditions under which this residual isolates the change induced by task supervision, and validate them empirically. Because the base is never directly modified, its broad capabilities remain available at inference, including behaviors such as recovery from failure that the demonstrations themselves do not exercise. Adaptation requires only forward velocity predictions from the base, making PPS lightweight to train and applicable even without access to the base’s parameters. On 8 real-world and 4 simulation manipulation tasks, PPS lifts the state-of-the-art π0.5 base policy by 55% absolute success rate on average, with zero-to-one gains on tasks the base never solves, while preserving the base’s broad capabilities. PPS outperforms LoRA fine-tuning, from-scratch specialists, residual policies, and prior inference-time steering methods.
tfC6LMD02z.k: Policy Steering, VLA Models, Flow-Matching Policy

k9EjTLL8bA.a: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are effective generalist robot controllers, but in long-horizon tasks a visually plausible action can be inappropriate unless earlier subgoals have been completed. We introduce historical support, a reliability criterion asking whether task history justifies a candidate action at the current decision step. Based on this criterion, RAMT-VLA keeps the base VLA frozen and adds a lightweight post-policy assessor that scores candidate action chunks, outputs sparse evidence masks for each candidate, and reranks candidates by historical support. The assessor is trained without dense evidence annotations using wrong-history and missing-evidence counterfactuals, with sparsity and faithfulness regularization. With a frozen 0.5B base model, RAMT-VLA achieves 98.1% average success on LIBERO, 83.3% on SimplerEnv-WidowX, and 84.0% on real-world long-horizon tasks. Matched LIBERO ablations, candidateselection controls, and transfer evaluations show that support-based reranking improves the frozen base policy, with the largest history-dependent gains on longhorizon tasks, beyond generic sampling or policy-confidence reranking.
k9EjTLL8bA.k: Vision-Language-Action Models, Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation, Reliability-Aware Action Selection

FFB8qNJwV2.a: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models generate action chunks for temporally coherent robot motion, but chunked control creates a fundamental closed-loop trade-off: long chunks provide smooth execution, whereas frequent replanning improves reactivity at the cost of action discontinuities. We introduce REACT, a rolling-denoising framework that makes flow-based VLAs more reactive while preserving long-horizon context. Instead of regenerating entire action chunks from scratch, REACT maintains a persistent action buffer with staggered flow timesteps. At each control step, the full horizon is denoised using the latest observation, the cleanest action block is executed, partially refined future blocks are shifted forward, and fresh noise is appended to the tail. As a result, each executed action block is refined across multiple recent observations before deployment. To support real-time control, we further introduce dual decoupling, which separates sensing, VLM encoding, DiT denoising, and action execution, enabling high-frequency observation updates and action streaming under practical compute constraints. Across the RoboTwin 2.0 simulation benchmark and real-world tasks spanning bimanual manipulation and dynamic control on multiple robot platforms, REACT improves task success and reduces reaction latency while producing smoother trajectories than frequent-replanning and asynchronous baselines.
FFB8qNJwV2.k: Reactive Robot Control, Vision-Language-Action Models, Flow Matching Project page: react-vla.github.io

VnF3D7ia9Y.a: When humans hand each other objects, they incorporate both geometric and semantic information into this process. For example, passing a knife with the handle towards the recipient, rather than the blade, is both more ergonomic and safer. Recent state-of-the-art methods for task-oriented robot-human handovers have progressed from modeling object geometry to incorporating object affordances. However, they often forgo predicting the explicit, task-specific hand poses a human selects to utilize an object. Since many objects support multiple interaction modalities, e.g., a claw hammer used to strike or pull nails, this variability must be modeled to achieve robust task-oriented handovers. To tackle this, we propose a novel approach, GENESIS-Handover (GENErative HypotheSIS), which leverages VLM image generation to produce a variety of task-specific hand-object interaction hypotheses. These hypotheses are matched in real time to the observed human hand pose, enabling inference of the most suitable handover configuration. By leveraging VLMs as priors of plausible hand-object interactions, the method produces task-conditioned handover strategies for previously unseen object-task pairs. We evaluate the standalone interaction proposal module before deploying the full system on a mobile manipulator. In a user study with 12 participants across five task-object pairs, 83.3% perceived our method to have better task understanding than the previous state of the art.
VnF3D7ia9Y.k: Human-Robot Interaction, Task-Oriented Handovers, Mobile Manipulation, Large Language Models, Vision Language Models, Image Generation

jlXzHOkSXq.a: Real-time execution, enabled by asynchronous inference that ensures both smooth action trajectories and fast reactivity, is critical for realistic deployments of large-scale Vision-Language-Action models. However, recent work on real-time execution primarily focuses on variants of diffusion policies, even though it is more critical for autoregressive policies given their slower rollout speed in synchronous inference. In contrast, we demonstrate that autoregressive policies can achieve real-time execution by adjusting the tokenization horizon and applying constrained decoding, thereby guaranteeing strict latency bounds that enable multitrajectory decoding to maximize performance. Across simulated and real-world environments, we find that the autoregressive policy consistently outperforms its equivalent-level flow-matching policy counterpart while achieving significantly improved task completion speeds from synchronous inference. Coupled with the inherent advantages of autoregressive policies, such as faster convergence and better generalizability in instruction-following, these results confirm that autoregressive policies can remain a competitive policy type supporting real-time execution.

P1R9iBKyv4.a: Spatial understanding is essential for robots to perceive their surrounding environments and execute actions. Existing approaches typically encode 3D awareness into vision-language-action (VLA) models by directly aligning their representations with pre-trained 3D foundation models. However, we observe that such direct geometric feature alignment essentially exploits 3D foundation priors as a form of low-rank regularization in the feature space, resulting in severe rank collapse of the pre-trained VLA representations. In contrast, we shift the focus from enforcing point-wise equality to aligning pair-wise relationships. We propose a representation-alignment method that enables the injection of 3D spatial awareness without compromising the model’s original expressivity. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks, our new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation scenarios demonstrate that our approach effectively incorporates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning, achieving robust performance and enhanced spatial awareness across diverse manipulation tasks.

1HqdYVWaXi.a: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable robots to follow openlanguage instructions. However, dense VLM embeddings have shown to be noisy and lack spatial consistency. This is problematic for robotic applications, which require simultaneous reasoning over semantics and 3D space. We examine spatial structure across recent VLMs and propose ReSiReg, a feature reconstruction method that uses spatially consistent VLM intermediates to improve dense language-grounded retrieval. ReSiReg clusters intermediates into visual prototypes, derives their language descriptors, and reconstructs each patch as a soft mixture of prototype-level language embeddings. We evaluate quantitatively on OVSS and 3D mapping across backbones, and qualitatively in real-world manipulation scenes. Quantitative results show improved dense retrieval; manipulation scenes show more spatially consistent target activations. We further provide a compact 25M dense VLM for robotic applications, substantially smaller than and competitive with ViT-B baselines. Available at https://resireg.github.io
1HqdYVWaXi.k: Vision Language Model, Semantic Mapping, Semantic Segmentation

RYXo2ktK1M.a: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can learn to perform diverse manipulation skills “out of the box,” but achieving the precision and speed realworld tasks demand requires further fine-tuning with reinforcement learning (RL). We introduce a lightweight method that enables sample-efficient online RL finetuning of pretrained VLAs using just a few hours of real-world practice. We (1) adapt the VLA to expose an “RL token,” a compact readout representation that preserves task-relevant pretrained knowledge while serving as an efficient interface for online RL, and (2) train a small actor-critic head on this RL token to refine the actions, while anchoring the learned policy to the VLA. Online RL with the RL token (RLT) makes it possible to fine-tune even large VLAs with RL quickly and efficiently. Across four real-robot tasks that demand millimeter-level precision, RLT improves the speed on the hardest part of the task by up to 3× and raises success rates significantly within minutes to a few hours of practice. It can even surpass human teleoperation speed on some of the tasks.

db6WHoqH91.a: Enhancing the generalization of robotic learning in diverse unseen environments remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches often rely on large-scale pretraining, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming, or semantic data augmentation methods that assume flawless upstream object detection in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose RoboAug, a novel generative data augmentation framework that reduces reliance on large-scale pretraining and perfect visual recognition by requiring only a single image with bounding box annotations for dataset construction. Leveraging this minimal supervision, RoboAug employs pretrained generative models for precise semantic augmentation and introduces a plug-and-play region-contrastive loss to guide attention toward taskrelevant regions, thereby enhancing generalization and task success rates. Extensive real-world experiments on UR-5e, AgileX, and Tian Gong 2.0 demonstrate that RoboAug consistently outperforms state-of-the-art augmentation baselines under background, distractor, and lighting shifts. Our project is available at https://x-roboaug.github.io/.
db6WHoqH91.k: Robot Learning, Imitation Learning, Perception, Data Augmentation

A9AQjk3dAt.a: Modern embodied agents achieve impressive success rates, yet their actual instruction-following ability is far weaker than these numbers suggest. We trace this illusion to a structural property we term low scene entropy: when a visual scene admits only one valid task, language becomes redundant and a policy can score highly while barely using it. We introduce RoboFollow, a diagnostic benchmark with three principles: (1) High Scene Entropy: each training scene supports multiple kinematically distinct task branches, making vision alone insufficient and forcing reliance on language. (2) Hierarchical Diagnostic Protocol: a four-level protocol (L0–L3) progressively perturbs visual layout and semantics, probing whether equivalent instructions yield consistent behavior and distinct ones yield discriminable behavior across spatial relations, attributes, trajectory constraints, and logic. (3) Confound-Controlled Diagnosis: we simplify interaction objects, restrict actions to the trained repertoire and report stagewise Intent and Execution scores, isolating comprehension from motor execution. Evaluation of nine VLA and WAM policies shows that strong L0 performance, where attained, does not reliably transfer to L1–L3 under our fine-tuning setup. Representative mitigations, including stronger VLM backbones, QA co-training, LangForce, and Classifier-Free Guidance, all fail to close this gap. RoboFollow exposes genuine instruction following as a critical, overlooked bottleneck. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/RoboFollow and https://huggingface.co/datasets/AutoLab-SJTU/robofollow-data.
A9AQjk3dAt.k: Embodied Artificial Intelligence, Vision-Language-Action Models, World Action Models, Instruction Following

xMysKLF2hX.a: Estimating the performance of a robot’s control policy before real-world deployment typically relies on rollout-based approaches, which execute the policy in a simulator or in a learned world model. Both approaches are costly to construct: simulators require extensive domain expertise, while world models require large-scale training infrastructure and additionally suffer from prediction errors that compound over the evaluation horizon. To address these challenges, we leverage off-policy evaluation (OPE), a framework that estimates the return of a target policy from a fixed dataset of offline trajectories. OPE has been studied primarily on lowdimensional, state-based tasks, and its effectiveness for visuomotor robot control remains largely unexplored. To make OPE practical in this setting, we introduce RoboFQE, which fits a Q-function to offline trajectories, without ever rolling out the policy. RoboFQE leverages a pretrained vision foundation model to handle highdimensional inputs and a learned terminal success detector to supply reward signals without labels. Through experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, we demonstrate that RoboFQE produces reliable return estimates, significantly outperforming world-model evaluators by a growing margin as the evaluation horizon increases. We further show that the pretrained vision foundation model is critical for RoboFQE on long-horizon tasks, while the learned success detector eliminates the need for ground-truth reward labels with minimal loss in accuracy.

uizBY3yrgz.a: The pursuit of general-purpose robotic manipulation is hindered by the scarcity of diverse, real-world interaction data. Unlike the large-scale web vision-language data, robotic data collection is an active process incurring prohibitive physical costs. As a result, the key challenge is not merely to collect more robot data, but to obtain training data that provides informative learning knowledge by broadening behavioral coverage and capturing meaningful variations in objects, scenes, and skills. However, how to automatically curate task proposals that maximize the utility of collected robot data remains a critical yet under-explored challenge. To address this, we introduce RoboGene, an agentic framework designed to automate the generation of diverse and informative manipulation tasks across heterogeneous robotic embodiments, spanning single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile robots. RoboGene integrates three core components: (1) diversity-driven sampling for broad task coverage, (2) agentic self-reflection for task-quality assessment, and (3) human-verified feedback memory for executiongrounded validation and continual refinement. We conduct extensive quantitative analysis and large-scale real-world experiments, collecting datasets of 18k trajectories and introducing novel metrics to assess task quality in terms of feasibility and diversity. Results demonstrate that RoboGene significantly outperforms frontier foundation models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro). Furthermore, realworld experiments show that VLA models trained on data generated by RoboGene achieve higher success rates and stronger generalization, highlighting the importance of high-quality task generation. Our project page and dataset are publicly available at robogene-boost-vla.github.io, with dataset repositories hosted on Hugging Face and ModelScope.
uizBY3yrgz.k: Robot Learning, Vision-Language-Action Models, Task Generation

Q4ehHMIPmb.a: Long-horizon embodied tasks require agents to learn, reason, and generalize robustly across complex real-world environments. However, existing approaches often struggle with partial observability, fragmented spatial reasoning, and inefficient integration of heterogeneous memories, limiting their capacity for long-horizon adaptation. To address this, we introduce RoboMemory, a braininspired framework that unifies Temporal, Spatial, Semantic, and Episodic memory for efficient long-horizon planning and interactive learning. Its core innovations are a comprehensive memory system designed for embodied tasks, and a dynamic spatial knowledge graph for scalable, consistent memory updates. Extensive experiments on EmbodiedBench show that RoboMemory improves the average success rate of Qwen2.5-VL-72B-Ins by 26.5 percentage points and achieves performance comparable to strong closed-source VLM agents. Real-world trials further suggest RoboMemory’s potential for interactive environmental learning by reusing accumulated experience across repeated task attempts. These results demonstrate RoboMemory as a scalable memory-augmented framework for embodied agents, improving long-horizon planning and cumulative learning in complex interactive environments.
Q4ehHMIPmb.k: Task and motion planning, Memory, Embodied Agent

NHE9q2cz1n.a: Recent robot foundation models operate with single-step or shorthistory visuomotor context. We introduce Test-Time-Training Robot Policies (ROBOTTT), a robot model and training recipe that scale visuomotor context to 8K timesteps, three orders of magnitude beyond state-of-the-art policies, without growing inference latency. At this context length, we unlock new robot capabilities: one-shot in-context imitation from human video demonstrations, on-the-fly policy improvement, robustness to perturbations, and stronger performance on multi-stage, long-horizon tasks. We also observe, for the first time, steady gains in closed-loop performance as pretraining context length scales. At its core, ROBOTTT integrates Test-Time Training into robot foundation models such as Vision-Language-Action policies, yielding a sequence model whose recurrent state consists of fast weights, parameters updated by gradient descent during both training and inference, compressing histories into weight space and retrieving contextual information for long-context conditioning. To scale training context length, the recipe combines sequence action forcing with truncated backpropagation through time. On challenging real-robot manipulation tasks, ROBOTTT improves overall performance by 87% over the single-step context baseline and fully completes a five-minute, ten-stage assembly task, which no baseline ever does. ROBOTTT trained with 8K-timestep context outperforms the same model pretrained with 1K timesteps by 62%, suggesting context length as a new scaling axis for robot foundation models. Project website: research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/robottt.
NHE9q2cz1n.k: Long-Context Policies, Test-Time Training, Robot Foundation Models

Xgth4qBOmb.a: Safe control is a prerequisite for real-world embodied intelligence, for which safe reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising paradigm. However, existing safe reinforcement learning methods either require costly realworld exploration or depend on hand-crafted safety functions. Neither scales to vision-language-action models deployed in open-world physical environments. We propose SafeDojo, a model-based safe reinforcement learning framework that improves vision-language-action policies through world-model imagination. SafeDojo performs online reinforcement learning on top of an interactive video world model. A ResNet success classifier scores predicted future frames, while a lightweight safety head predicts per-step contact probabilities from the current latent context and proposed action chunk, jointly assessing task execution and trajectory safety. These decoupled signals are balanced through Lagrangian-constrained GRPO. On SafeLIBERO Level I, SafeDojo improves average safe-success rate by 8.25 percentage points over the strongest baseline; on the zero-shot Level II setting, it is competitive with the strongest model-free baseline. Real-world Franka deployment further shows the best average task and safe-success rates across five tasks. These results support world-model-based safe reinforcement learning as a promising path toward safer embodied intelligence.
Xgth4qBOmb.k: Safe Reinforcement Learning, Vision-Language-Action, World Model SafeDojo Overview

Z04KxYWC6V.a: Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for language-conditioned robotic manipulation, but their reliance on 2D visual backbones limits precise reasoning about depth, spatial relations, and contact-rich actions. We propose SAGE-3D, a semantic-aware 3D VLA framework that aligns geometric structure with task semantics for instruction-conditioned action prediction. Motivated by representation analysis, our key insight is that effective 3D VLA policies require both transferable geometric cues and instruction-relevant semantic grounding: geometry should not be injected as an isolated modality, but organized around objects, relations, and affordances relevant to the task. To realize this, SAGE-3D introduces a 3D Semantic-Aware Feature Generator (SAFG), which integrates RGB semantics, depth information, and task instructions to produce 3D Reasoning Tokens. These tokens are injected into the action head through a FiLM-based geometry-conditioned decoder, allowing semanticaware spatial context to directly modulate action generation. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world manipulation show that SAGE-3D improves overall benchmark performance and training efficiency, with the largest gains on spatially demanding tasks. Notably, SAGE-3D reaches 100% success on LIBERO-S PATIAL, establishing a new state-of-the-art result and, to our knowledge, the first result to saturate this benchmark. Anonymous code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/SAGE3D. 21

bL51SsKShM.a: Real-world evaluation of generalist robot policies is bottlenecked by manual resets, human grading, and small fixed task suites with limited diagnostic coverage. We present S CALE E VALS, a scalable reset-free protocol that evaluates policies through continuous physical play across a robot fleet. A VLM AutoPrompter generates scene-grounded tasks with difficulty estimates, language prompts, and skill tags, enabling performance analysis across diverse rollouts. A VLM AutoGrader assesses task progress, achieving 90.7% agreement with human graders. Scores are aggregated via a soft-win Bradley–Terry model, while tagstratified ANOVA provides interpretable capability diagnostics. Across 3,000+ physical autonomous rollouts on DROID and YAM, S CALE E VALS achieves 23.0 net rollouts/hr per station while reducing active human labor by 98%. By ranking five SOTA generalist policies, S CALE E VALS correlates with held-out manual evaluation ranking on DROID (r=0.94, p=0.018) and YAM (r=0.839, ρ=0.800). Beyond aggregate rankings, we observe behavioral compositionality: recombining verb-, skill-, and object-conditioned evidence predicts policy order on unseen prompts. Across 10 tasks and 240 prospective physical rollouts, we recover threepolicy orderings of 96% pairwise concordance, demonstrating S CALE E VALS can predict not just which policy leads, but where rankings reverse. Project: scaleevals.github.io
bL51SsKShM.k: Generalist Robot Policy Evaluation, Scalability, Benchmark

z5Mgc1GGjP.a: The strong performance of large vision–language models (VLMs) trained with reinforcement learning (RL) has motivated similar approaches for finetuning vision–language–action (VLA) models in robotics. Many recent works finetune VLAs directly in the real world to avoid addressing the sim-to-real gap. While real-world RL circumvents sim-to-real issues, it inherently limits the generality of the resulting VLA, as scaling scene and object diversity in the physical world is prohibitively difficult. This leads to the paradoxical outcome of transforming a broadly pretrained model into an overfitted, scene-specific policy. Training in simulation can instead provide access to diverse scenes, but designing those scenes is also costly. In this work, we show that VLAs can be RL fine-tuned across broad scene and object distributions and with reduced labor by leveraging 3D world generative models. Using these models together with a language-driven scene designer, we generate 100 diverse interactive scenes containing unique objects and backgrounds, enabling scalable and highly parallel policy learning. Starting from a pretrained imitation baseline, our approach increases simulation success from 9.7% up to 79.8% while achieving a 1.25× speedup in task completion time. We further demonstrate successful sim-to-real transfer enabled by the quality of the generated scenes together with domain randomization, improving real-world success from 21.7% to 75% and achieving a 1.13× speedup. Finally, we further highlight the benefits of leveraging the effectively unlimited data from 3D world generative models through an ablation study showing that increasing scene diversity directly improves zero-shot generalization. Video results are available at our project page.
z5Mgc1GGjP.k: Sim-to-Real RL, VLA, Robot Manipulation, Generative Simulation

rYkaehgzzO.a: Generalization remains a central bottleneck for vision-language-action (VLA) models: under distractors, appearance shifts, and semantically similar tasks, the policy must often infer local execution details from coarse instructions while also deciding which parts of the image matter for control. We present S2 (See Less, Specify More), a framework for improving VLA generalization by training the executor under a cleaner interface. Specify More preserves the original instruction as a stable high-level goal while relabeling each trajectory into refined trajectory- and subtask-level language that disambiguates the current execution mode. Unlike native attention, See Less imposes an explicit visual evidence budget, training the executor to act from task-sufficient evidence rather than unconstrained visual context, without any region or mask annotation.
